maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Prime Minister took exception to some four or five questions which I placed on the order paper, and I submit that his objections were entirely out of order.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext: The ruling has been made and is not debatable. It can be appealed from, but the time has passed for that.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext: I would refer you, Mr. Speaker, to Beauchesne at page 342.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext: That is coming exactly to the point I mentioned yesterday. I did pot base my ruling on the commentaries of Beauchesne ; I based it on standing order 44, which clearly .states that no question involving an argument can be placed on the order paper. Perhaps my hon. friend would discuss this matter with me privately; this is hardly the time for it.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext:
On a question of privilege and point of order, I assert the right of a private member to ask questions of the ministry. Standing order No. 1, as found in Beauchesne is as follows:
In all cases not provided for hereinafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this house.
I submit that it is the duty of the ministry to answer these questions as far as may be
Privilege-Mr. Church

possible. In Great Britain there is a standing older which provides that questions which may not appear on the order paper but which are of an urgent character or which refer to matters of public importance or to the conduct of public business may be asked. Acting upon this rule, the members practically crossexamine the ministry.
In a new book on parliamentary procedure published last summer by G. F. H. Campion, Second Clerk Assistant of the British House of Commons, I read the following:
Not later than three o'clock the question hour begins. This is a more important item of business than any yet described. It is expected to provide lively moments and seems to be of unfailing interest to members and the public. It is modern and affords a useful method of supervising the administration of the government. Its effectiveness is generally recognized. Questions "turn a searchlight upon every corner of the public service" (Lowell, 1. 332). Their chief object is "the explanation to the public of the meaning of political events," and "they are often arranged by the government itself so as to give them an opportunity of making announcements in a somewhat informal way" (Redlich, ii, 241 and 242). They are "serviceable as obviating the necessity in many instances of more extended debate and of motions for papers" (Todd, 1882. ii. 85). And finally "Questions afford to the private member under modern conditions almost his only opportunity" (Marriott, i, 571).
I would refer again to the fact that under standing order 1, in all cases not provided for in our rules the usages and customs of the British house as in force at the time will be followed. I do not see why I should be ruled out of order. I might point out that there are three very convenient ways of answering questions:	The first is "no information"; the
second is, "wait and see," the words of Mr. Asquith; the third is "announcement will be made in due course". One question with regard to unemployment, which was ruled out of order was answered in almost exactly the same terms in twTo previous sessions, and the answer was that it was a matter for the provinces and municipalities. I desire to assert my right to ask these questions under these rules and usages both of this house and the British House of Commons.
They are not. the set answers which the opposition should expect under the rules of this honourable house. "No information" is the reply given as to those soldiers of the great war appointed to the Senate and the high court bench of thp provinces; although information is in the parliamentary guide and the answ'er should have been "none". In the British House of Commons when Mr. Winston Churchill was not satisfied with such a reply as that made by Mr. Snowden regarding cer-

tain matters which had been raised in the house, he was sustained in his objection, and the information was forced from the chancellor. Under the rule supplementary questions can be asked all over the British chamber. Standing order No. 1 of this house is that the rules of the British House of Commons shall be applied as far as aipplicable to this house. I would ask Mr. Speaker to study these authorities, perhaps later on, because this is a very important matter, and give a decision. The authorities cited from Todd's twelfth edition, set out in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, paragraphs 342 and 349, page 113, have been modified, by the new series of rules on questions adopted by the British House of Commons, which, under our standing order No. 1, are binding on this honourable house.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member need not hand up the volume because I read it during the recess, having received it direct from England. I may say to the hon. member that he was right in rising at this time. I gather that he had no intention of appealing from the ruling given yesterday, as he rose on a question of privilege, and he was right in doing that.
I would remind the hon. gentleman that I know of the existence of standing order No. 1, which reads:
In all cases not provided for hereinafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this house.
I would draw attention to the two riders, "not provided for" and "so far as they may be applicable to this house." We have standing order 44. which I read to the house when these questions were put, and it states in part: -but in putting any such question or in reply-' ing to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the same.
The matter would be different if the government were refusing to answer a clear cut question, but when the question is argumentative, surely I am bound by our standing order.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders
of the day are proceeded with, a question touching upon the privileges of parliament is now under discussion. I conceive it to be in accordance with British and Canadian practice for a private member to place upon the order paper questions touching upon the conduct of public affairs. The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Church) has directed attention to the observations in that regard of Campion, who refers to the works of Lowell and Redlich as to the right, not only of private members and of the opposition, but of the government itself to present facts to the house through the medium of questions. As to the form in which these questions are to be asked, it seems to me that there is no doubt at all that the rules cover that point, and that the questions must be capable of being directly answered. The government is not bound in any sense to anticipate its policy in answering a question. I think that is clear, but there are other questions, questions which are asked orally before the orders of the day are proceeded with. Such questions usually refer to matters of urgent public concern, and it has been the custom usually, if the matter is of great importance, for the member asking the question to submit a copy of it either to the Prime Minister or the responsible head of the department which might be affected by the question. During the last few days questions have been asked which, it seems to me were susceptible of a very simple answer, and rather than it being said that they were improperly asked, the government might very well say, "We will take the matter under consideration."
I submit that the privileges of parliament are such that any member has a right to direct attention to a matter of public concern before the orders of the day are proceeded with. The subject matter of the question may be of such a character that the government may not care to discuss it, and might reply, " This matter will receive our consideration and attention," or, " our purpose will be made known as the session proceeds," or as the case may be. I would draw attention to the clear distinction between the right of a member to ask a question and the right of the government to dispose of it in any way it sees fit. The government's answer may be of such a character as to afford no information, depending upon the importance of the question, the character of the results which follow from the answer which may ge biven, and other factors to which I will not refer at this time.
I venture to take up this matter at this time as being one which touches upon the great privileges of parliament as they affect matters of public interest. If I may give an illustration without transgressing the rules: The question asked by the hon. member for West Essex (Mr. Robinson) touched upon a matter of very grave international importance. It seems to me that the question itself was in order but that the Prime Minister might very properly, and I think perhaps that others in his place would have said, " This is a matter of serious moment and in due course we will endeavour to give you an answer." I give that illustration to accentuate what I conceive to be the clear distinction between the right to ask a question, as a matter of it being in order, and the right of the government to decline to give a specific answer because of the lack of opportunity to consider implications which might arise from the answer, and the interests which might be involved.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the government is concerned we are not only willing but most anxious to answer any questions which may be asked for the purpose of obtaining information. I think more latitude has been allowed with respect to questions which have been asked lately on the orders of the day than has been the customary practice in this parliament. There are certain rules which it is to the advantage of the house as a whole to have observed. If, when the orders of the day are called, members are to be permitted to read extracts from newspapers and consume the time of the house by so doing, it will simply mean the delay of orders upon the paper, which should be dealt with promptly in the regular way. The leader of the opposition has given as an example the question just put by the hon. member for West Essex. The hon. member read a long extract from a newspaper and I confess, although I was able to follow the first part of it, that before he got to the end I had not the remotest idea to what part of the newspaper item he was going to refer. I do not think the reading of the article was the correct procedure, but if it was a very urgent matter the hon. member might have done as his leader has suggested, and come to me, or sent a note to my secretary before the house met, saying that he intended to ask a question. Had that been done, I would have endeavoured to be in a position to reply, but the very fact that the question was, as my hon. friend has suggested, one involving international conditions, will, I am
Privilege-Mr. Church

sure, cause my hon. friend himself to appreciate why the answer to the question should not have been given offhand.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext: From listening to the press quotation, it would appear that it refers to something which had been done by a municipality in another country. If I had answered offhand, I would have said, "It seems to me that what municipalities in other countries do or do not do is their business and not ours," but I would not have liked to have made that reply offhand. I am quite prepared to deal in a fair way with any question on the order paper, but I think the government must ask you, Mr. Speaker, to assist the house in observing its own rules with respect to the form in which questions are put and the amount of latitude to be allowed in asking general questions; in other words, in seeking by asking a question to give information to the house rather than to obtain information from the minister.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH RULES AND PROCEDURE RELATING TO QUESTIONS
speechtext:
In reference to the Canadian practice, Bourinot at page 354, speaking on calling of orders, says:
It is a practice, sanctioned by usage but not by any ipositive rule, for members in both houses of the Canadian parliament to make personal explanations or ask questions of the government when the orders of the day are called. They make them in reference to an inaccurate report of their speeches in the official record, or in the newspapers; or in denial of certain charges made against them in the public prints; or in reference to certain remarks which had been misunderstood on a previous occasion, and which they had not before had an opportunity of explaining; or in respect to delay in obtaining returns or to the incompleteness or inaccuracy of certain returns brought down under the order of the house. But these remarks are not allowable on the ground of privilege, unless the conduct of a member as such is attacked, and in that case a motion should be formally proposed.
Therefore, the Canadian practice is well laid down in Bourinot, but as a matter of courtesy I allow membei's to put brief and concrete questions to the government, and generally the government answers them. As a matter of practice, however, no involved questions should be put before the orders of the day are called, such questions must be preceded by ftotice, on the order paper, otherwise much valuable time would be lost before the sitting really began.

subtopic: DISABILITIES DUE TO WAR SERVICE-ONUS OP DISPROOF ON PENSION BOARD

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, February 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Peter McGibbon (Muskoka-Ontario):
That, in the opinion of this house, any exsoldier who has served in any theatre of war, who applies for a pension or an increase of pension and submits evidence or an opinion from any reputable physician or surgeon in Canada, stating that his disability is directly or indirectly attributable to war services, the onus of disproof shall be upon the Board of Pension Commissioners and that unless the same be disproved a pension shall be granted to the said applicant in accordance with the schedule at present in force under the regulations of the Board of Pension Commissioners.

subtopic: DISABILITIES DUE TO WAR SERVICE-ONUS OP DISPROOF ON PENSION BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing the debate, I hope I shall not be long. Since last we discussed this motion and the amendment to it, some water-I wish it had been more-has passed under I he bridge. We have the War Veterans Allowances Act. So far as that act confers benefits upon returned soldiers in response from us to the obligation incurred by us, it has my whole-hearted support; I commend it and I believe the people of the country commend it. But the point is that first things should be dealt with first. When the soldiers left our shores they left under a bargain. It was a bargain where the proponent, the country, acted voluntarily and it was cheerfully agreed to by the people. A response has to be made to our duty in relation to that contract, for such it is, and the question of the Pension Act and its administration should be first dealt with. Why? I try to put myself into the position of the soldier. I have gone under the conditions that the soldiers of Canada have gone under. I have come back. I have earned a pension. I say that that pension is the w'hite flower and decoration of patriotic service. It is valuable; it is a grant that comes from His Majesty and to which I am entitled. I wear it proudly and it is of value because it sustains me. That is not the principle of the War Veterans Allowances Act. If the result of this measure is going to be-and I emphasize the word "if"- that soldiers who are entitled to pension are to be asked to take a veteran's allowance without the pension, I object.
I said on the former occasion that I was in favour of the principle of the motion and of the amendment. I am still, and frankly I do not know how the house and the country are going to move away from the principle of the amendment. Not to take up time, let me ask: What is that principle? Shortly

War Pensions-Mr. Ryckman
stated, it is this that if a veteran makes out
a prima facie case that he should have a pension, then the onus is on the crown or the pension board or its officers to establish that that veteran is not entitled to a pension. It often happens in a court of justice that a prima facie case has been made out and the jury give their verdict on it. Sometimes objection is taken that there is not sufficient evidence to support the verdict and sometimes that succeeds, because there is not. But when there is enough evidence given by a veteran to support his claim, if it were being tried oy a jury, then I say that the onus should be shifted and should be lifted from the shoulders of the soldier. That is a principle all through our jurisprudence, and as I tried to point out when I spoke last, it has occurred in eases where the liberty of the subject is at stake. No one has objected to it.
I heard one hon. gentleman, speaking on the other side, say he did not just know, but he had an open mind and he could be converted. I believe that is the. effect of what he said. I have some friends on the other side of the house, and I have others who, I think, would like to oblige me. We have debated this matter for four days. Now will they summarize it and tell us what is wrong with this suggestion? Supposing the question comes to me: Why do you insist upon that principle? Why do you object to the matter going to the committee? I do not object to this going to the committee, but what I want is to have a mandate go to the committee sajdng that the house, which is greater than the committee, for the whole is greater than any part, having considered this matter for four days has come to the conclusion that the principle as to shifting the onus should be passed on to the committee as fixed and that the committee should govern itself accordingly. If there is some valid objection, I should like to hear it. I shall be glad to say that I am wrong if there is some countervailing reason against this principle being followed.
Again, why do I want this? Two years ago a committee was appointed at the beginning of the session.. It dealt earnestly and profitably with the question, but it reported in the last hours of the session. My hon. leader proposed an amendment, and across the floor of this house he said to the Minister of Pensions: Let us have this and we will be satisfied. The minister replied; No, we have made good progress on this bill, and that is all we can do now.

When six o'clock came last night I
had almost finished what I wanted to say on the presentation of the resolution asking for the setting up of professorships and scholarships on international affairs in loading universities in Canada. I had just been saying we would all agree that the Rhodes scholarships had done very much to weld the empire into one unit, and I believe that international scholarships, if carried out in many countries, could do much the same for international relations. Undoubtedly if we had students from abroad studying in Canada, and Canadian students studying abroad, they would all under-

International Peace-Miss Macphail
stand international affairs much better than before they had gone out of their own country. This would have a tendency to humanize international relations by an increase of mutual knowledge and appreciation.
A committee or a commission could look after the giving of the scholarships, as was the case with the Rhodes scholarships. The selection of the students and the choosing of the professors would undoubtedly rest with the board of governors of the universities. There is a precedent for giving scholarships to students in other parts of the world. The French government offers each year scholarships in this country and I know of students who went to study in France, and who did so because of the generosity of the French government. They undoubtedly came back to Canada with a much greater knowledge of France and possibly a much wider knowledge of world affairs than they had before they left our shores.
The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) is known not only in oui own country, but also abroad, as a scholar, a man who has held learning high, and I think nothing could be more fitting than that it should be known that the government which he leads relies on education as a means of attaining security. Organizations like the League of Nations and declarations like the Kellogg pact and, indeed, treaties of peace and arbitration generally, need not be expected to be really effective unless they are backed by popular opinion; and if popular opinion is to be steady and sane and sound, it must be educated.
I want again in closing to say that I do not wish to press for the exact wording of the resolution where it says "in each Canadian university". It is simply the general idea that we should have the study of international relationships in leading universities that I am interested in. I wrote to many professors and heard from a good many. One of them outlined the universities that he thought might well be given chairs, and the number was twelve. That would be one for Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, one in New Brunswick, three in Quebec, three in Ontario, and one each in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. To do that would not be very expensive and I appeal to the members of the house to remember that if we are going to have peace, we must prepare for it. I feel that this would be a step in that direction. I feel, too, that matters pertaining to peace and war came under the jurisdiction of the federal government, and I can see no real argument against my proposal. I want the house to prepare itself for this argument, that
the Dominion government cannot interfere with the provinces. Apart from that there does not seem to me to be any argument against the motion. I believe it is a step in the right direction and I ask all the members of the house to support it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
With the principle underlying the
resolution, which principle, of course, is the promotion of peace, I am indeed highly in accord. The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) is a noble advocate of peace, and I congratulate her. There has been a change in the world during the last few years and it is no longer the part of a dreamer or a sign of inferiority to talk peace. Indeed, the dominating question in the world to-day is international peace. The last war worked so many injuries and caused so much damage that all men, however biased they may be, however rooted in the traditions of the past, are not prepared to begin all over again. War has shown conclusively that it does not pay anybody any longer. If those who are vanquished are crushed and ruined, the position of the winners is not very much better. Why, then, should we rebuild if everything is going to be destroyed again? Why devote energies to creating productive arts, works and functions if there are still threats of war pending that may pull that all down?
The old system has failed, as my hon. friend has said, and a new structure is being built, I hope on a basis of justice and solidarity. That is why new institutions have been created and are now doing splendid work. The League of Nations is no longer an idea; it has become a reality and its strength is continuously increasing. In that League of Nations, not only are all the peoples of the world, except a few, meeting on a footing of equality, but men see to-day that those beyond the boundaries of their country are not merely possible enemies, but human beings with whom they can deal and transact business. The activities of the league manifest themselves in all spheres-in legal and constitutional questions, arbitrations, reduction of armaments, financial, industrial and economic problems in their international aspects, agriculture, shipping, transportation, health, social problems, and the protection of minorities. I think it would be interesting to some Canadians to know the measures which the league is taking for the protection of minorities. If we must promote peace abroad, it is a good thing to promote it at home too.
Apart from the assembly of the league itself, there is the council which deals with

International Peace-Mr. Lapointe
the larger problems. There, again, our country is playing an important part. We have our representatives on the council of the League of Nations, and certainly they have done credit to Canada. We have also the international labour bureau, which has done very effective work for the promotion of industrial peace, and industrial peace is certainly important for the maintenance of political and international peace. There, again, our country is playing an important part, being represented on the board of management by reason of the fact that we are one of the eight largest industrial countries of the world. Labour is also represented on that bureau, where Mr. Tom Moore is certainly considered as one of the most able and efficient representatives of labour in the world. There have been many arbitration treaties as between countries. I might mention particularly the pan-American treaty which was signed a couple of years ago. We have also had the Kellogg pact outlawing war. There, again, we were represented and our country has been a party to that pact. There is sitting in London at the present time a conference on naval disarmament, which we hope will reach a successful conclusion notwithstanding all the obstacles in the way. At that conference Canada is also represented.
During the course of last year Canada, in common with the other nations of the British Commonwealth, signed the optional clause of the statute of the international court of justice. That was a very important step, and may I add, with a certain amount of pride, that Canada assumed a position of leadership in the British Commonwealth so far as the signing of the optional clause is concerned, because before the other nations of the commonwealth, including the mother country, were prepared to sign that clause, Canada was prepared, and made that known to the rest of the empire.
We have, therefore, so far as the promotion of peace in the world is concerned, an international machinery in which Canada is interested and is playing an important part, machinery which is an obstacle to possible wars, and which is destined to settle disputes between nations. That machinery is not only the assembly and the council of the League of Nations, but also the international court of justice. In the second place, there is now manifesting itself in the world a new spirit, a new international conscience to which all nations of the world, even the most powerful, must have regard.
I have stated all this to indicate that so far as the promoting of peace is concerned, 
I am in full accord with the aims of my hon. friend from Southeast Grey, and I would do all in my power to help spread the doctrine of peace. As my hon. friend said yesterday, there must be a technique of peace as there is a technique of war. In the same way that there is an organization for war, it is a good thing that there should be an organization for peace. Having said that, I am afraid that I shall have to differ to some extent from nay hon. fniend. Being very shrewd, she foresaw that yesterday when she said she was expecting that somebody on the government side would talk about provincial rights in connection with this matter that that was their stock-in-trade argument, which she heard even in her sleep. I am not sure that this is altogether fair on the part of my hon. friend. I cannot help thinking that it must emanate from a remnant of that former state of mind prior to her submitting herself to the medical intervention of which she spoke to us last week, and which has had the effect of improving an already very agreeable temper; but surely she will grant me some measure of sincerity, as I am pleased to grant her the full measure of that virtue. She is in favour of international trust and good will. I hope that she will give me and the government at least a little of that trust and good wil.

subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Thank you; I am almost tempted to conclude my remarks right there.
For sixty years we have been building an organized state in order that we may live in Canada happily in prosperity and in peace. We have been building that state upon fundamental principles which cannot and should not lightly be interfered with. The sovereignty of the Canadian people operates in various fields of activity. It operates through the federal government in the matters which have been entrusted to the federal government by the constitution; it operates through the provincial governments in the matters which have been entrusted to the management and administration of those governments; it operates even through the municipal authorities in certain matters which have been given to their care and management. They are the same Canadian people, but it has -been considered better that this sovereignty should be exercised in those various fields.
Now, some are impatient on account of that situation, but Canada has been developing with that political condition, and the development is proceeding along pretty successfu

International Peace-Mr. Lapointe
and progressive lines. There are certain matters which, even if we would like to deal with them, should be dealt with by the provinces; other matters come under the jurisdiction and control of this parliament; and in the area which has been excluded from our federal activities no majority, however powerful it may be, has the right to go beyond that area. It would be the violation of an agreement, anid however desirable the purpose may be, if to succeed in that purpose you have to break agreements, I do not think it is a purpose which ought to be achieved. May I quote the words of Lord Stowell, which I think are applicable in this connection. He said:
To press forward to a great principle by breaking through every other principle that stands in the way of its establishment, is as little consonant to private morality as to public justice.
I Tepeat, certain 'boundaries have been established as to the respective jurisdictions and work of the federal parliament and the provinces, and if we trespass on the field which properly belongs to the other controlling governments we can only have chaos and disorder. So I do not think that talking of respecting the constitution should be considered a stigma of inferiority. Our country is built on federalism. In some respects it hampers certain developments. For instance, our friends of the labour unions, and the labour men in particular, are complaining that the conventions of the international labour bureau are not all ratified by Canada and should have been ratified by now. But the treaty itself creating the international labour bureau and conference provides that in federal states the duty of the central government is merely to transmit to the various states or provincial governments the conventions for their ratification. We cannot act in many other respects because of this federal system. We are not the only country in the world in this situation. Australia, a sister Dominion, is in exactly the same position, and the United States, Switzerland and many other countries are similarly situated.
I am not one of those who believe everything the fathers of confederation have done is perfect and should not be changed. I am not rooted to the past in any way, and I may assure mv hon. friend that when I am considering the solution of any problem I am not thinking either with the brains of my grandfather or with the brains of the grandfathers of anybody else. The problems of this century must certainly be looked at and solved in the light of the conditions which exist in the twentieth century. There are certain 2419-22
matters, I am free to admit, that perhaps the fathers of confederation would have settled otherwise than they did if they were living to-day. But may I say to my hon. friend and to those who are rather impatient and inclined to think as she does, that to come to the situation where it will be possible to effect those changes it is better to respect the agreements. The changes must be made by respecting the rights and the views of the other parties that may be concerned in the making of the changes, and to preach that we should not be trammelled or prevented from doing something which under the constitution we should not do, I am afraid gives arguments to those who are opposed to all changes, and I am not one of them. I submit-and I am Sony that I have perhaps dwelt too long on this aspect of the question-I submit that we must remain within our own sphere.

By a request from the provinces or by negotiations of some kind a way might be found to effect the purpose of the resolution. But I would direct attention to another difficulty. May I say with regard to the resolution itself, my hon. friend proposes that we should devote to the purpose which she indicates one dollar of every one hundred spent for war preparations. In the session of 1928 she had a resolution on the order paper that the time had come for the establishment of a government department for the promotion of peace, and in the debate on that resolution she said she would be satisfied for the time being if one hundredth part of the amount which was expended for military preparations every year were expended in promoting international peace and good will. Well, as my hon. friend said yesterday, a dollar for every one hundred dollars provided for military preparations would form an amount of approximately $200,000. I must call the attention of the house to the fact that out of this amount of $20,000,000 in the estimates of the Department of National Defence there is an item of over $4,000,000 which is not really for military purposes. It is for civil air operations-flying operations

International Peace-Mr. Lapointe
for civil government departments in connection with aerial photographic surveys, forestry patrols, forestry and grain pests, transportation, and so forth. That would make it about $16,000,000. I have indicated many fields of activities of Canada in the promoting of peace, such as the League of Nations, the International Labour Conference, the disarmament conference, and activities of that kind. The amount expended by Canada during the fiscal year 1928-29 in connection with those various activities was $199,926.76, or, in round figures, $200,000. With regard to the concrete proposal for establishing chairs of international relationships and international scholarships, this would involve an intervention in the field of education by the Dominion government.

speechtext:
I would rather wait until the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is here to give the answer to my hon. friend. Let me say, however, that when the Minister of National Defence defended that before the house he convinced me, at all events, that it was not at all an interference in the field of education that it was merely encouraging physical culture and manly exercise.

But this cannot be said of the creation of chairs in universities. Would it be welcome? My hon. friend says at least one professor told her that the universities would welcome it. I am not so sure that it would be welcome in the different provinces or universities, on account of the danger that underlies it. Some of those universities are privately endowed; some are denominational, and some are provincial institutions; each is jealous of its freedom and independence, and each would certainly resent any attempt at control by the Dominion government over their curriculum, or in the matter of appointments. And surely if the Dominion government were to create chairs in universities there would be a presumption at least that they would have something to say in the appointments to those chairs.
There are twenty odd universities in Canada
I think my hon. friend said seventeen, but my figure would be twenty. What place in the curriculum of the universities would a course in international relationships occupy? In most of the universities that I know of, there are chairs for the teaching of history, political economy, and political science, all of which relate as much to peace as a chair of international relations; and some of the universities have a chair of international law. The lessons of peace are being brought into all those universities by the different professors, on subjects which certainly bear upon international relations. 1 do not think there is a body of men or women in Canada who are more zealous for peace, and for the teaching of peace, than the university and college professors. They are doing this work at the present time, and I am not sure that this responsibility is not better discharged by all of them as it is being discharged to-day than by having one man or woman to do it in a chair of international relationships.
The same thing applies to scholarships, and it is not the first time that our constitutional position has had something to do with the decision we have to reach in a matter of this kind. Only a few years ago a splendid institution was created in Paris for Canadian students. I have visited it myself two or three times. La Maison des Etudiants in Paris is one of the finest institutions of its kind. It is situated in the district where other nations also have their special home for students, and at the time it was created those who were the organizers of that splendid movement asked the Dominion of Canada to create scholarships there in the same way as my hon. friend suggests. The question was then debated

International Peace-Mr. Church
and fully considered. Nothing would have pleased us more at that time than to grant the request that was then made, because, if peace is achieved by people of one country meeting people of another, there is no better opportunity for doing so than in Paris, where students and young professional men and women from all countries of the world gather for periods of two or three years. We could not do it, however much we should have liked to do so, and we directed them to the various provinces. I am pleased to say that most of the provinces, if not all, have created scholarships there. I know Quebec and Ontario sent students to Paris by virtue of these scholarships, but this has been done by the provinces because we thought we could not do it.
I heartily endorse the statement that the schools, colleges and universities are splendid places in which to carry on the work of peace; there is no place where peace should be preached and advocated more than in the schools. Perhaps I might say that those who are responsible for that work in Canada might copy what is being done in certain European countries, where a propaganda is being conducted to have the school books changed in certain respects in order to eliminate everything leading to hatred and distrust as between nations, and where an effort has been carried on to direct the admiration of the young generation to the heroes of peace in as large a measure as their admiration always has been compelled for the heroes of war. There again, however, it is a provincial matter.
I am sure my hon. friend knows that I am very sincere in my desire to promote peace, and I really believe that a difference of opinion on certain details should not be taken as a means of dividing those who are really working for peace, as we are.

This is not a new subject, Mr. Speaker; we had the same resolution last year. Every year, as soon as parliament closes, this annual pilgrimage or pleasure trip to the League of Nations commences. We have just concluded about twelve years of peace, peace agreements, peace pacts and pacifist speeches in this chamber, and throughout the world, and the result is the utter failure of what Woodrow Wilson spoke of as open diplomacy.
The hon. member for Southeast Grey referred to the fact that $20,000,000 was spent in our military estimates. That is not the case; the militia estimates for the last fiscal year amounted to just over $11,000,000, so there is a difference of a mere trifle of $9,000,000. The hon. member suggests that the 2419-224
amount which would be realized under this resolution which she estimates at $200,000 should be used to establish some peace chairs in Canadian universities, or some more fads in Canadian universities. Dear knows there are enough fads and frills in Toronto university to-day. In the Canadian universities they have no time to trifle with peace pacts, peace chairs and so on. We have too many faddists in the University of Toronto to-day, too many people shouting peace from the house tops when there is no permanent peace. Of the $11,000,000 voted last year nearly $5,000,000 was devoted to the permanent force. The permanent force of this country is very largely a police force, an auxiliary and aid in maintaining law and order from Vancouver to Halifax. The expenditure for cadet services amounted to $500,000, and I may tell my hon. friend that in the province of Ontario the cadet services will be continued whether she likes it or not. I understand that she belongs to the Progressive party and to the United Farmers of Ontario. These two parties were wiped off the map in the last election, like the Patrons of Industry, and to-day they have neither a tombstone nor an epitaph to indicate the remains of their former glory.
We have just heard a speech by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who quite often follows his colleague the government leader of the Senate, who always shows up at the opening of this assembly in Geneva. That is nothing but a public joy ride, as it has been termed in the British House of Commons. Mr. George Bernard Shaw has written an article in which he refers to the large amount of money spent in what the leader of the opposition in England calls a joy ride, although I suppose "pleasure ride" is probably the better English term for it. The Minister of Justice has now joined the pacifists; I think he is running the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) a very close race for the honour of 'being chief pacifist of the Dominion. Last year he brought back in his brief case from this league, a new magna charta which was to be brought before the house and placed on the statute books of the country. However, when the press pointed out that it would interfere with the rights of the minorities and with the municipalities, it was strongly opposed and nothing more was heard of this magnificent bill.
W'e should not talk about peace chairs in universities when the students of our colleges have enough to do to look for jobs during the Christmas and midsummer vacations. With all this nonsense about peace we are further away from it than we were before the great war. Even the name of Cecil Rhodes has

International Peace-Mr. Church
been brought into this discussion. Rhodes was a strong imperialist who 'believed in preparedness. If there was one man who believed Lord Roberts was right, it was Cecil Rhodes. I believe the people of this country are becoming sick and tired of the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars on the League of Nations. To-day Canada has the lowest expenditure on militia of almost any country in the world and the highest expenditure for the League of Nations, or, as I called it last year, the league of humbug and hypocrisy. The United States, who started this league, will not even join it. That country' trotted out the Kellogg note, but at the present disarmament conference that note has not been even mentioned. The Monroe doctrine is just a scrap of paper, as is the Kellogg note; it means nothing and nothing will come out of it.
The mover of the resolution says that the provinces should have something to say about this matter. They will because Canada is not going to be talked1 out of the British Empire; Canada will have to be fought out of that empire.
The resolution asks that one dollar be spent on peace for every one hundred dollars spent on war purposes. Not one dollar is spent by this country for war, and not one dollar has been spent for that purpose during any fiscal year since I have been a member of
the house. Money spent for cadet training is not spent for war, it is spent for athletics and the physical development of youth, and the athletic directors of the country heartily support this cadet movement which teaches respect for authority.

Expenditures for militia never have been considered as being a war measure. That is where the pacificists make a mistake; they believe that disarmament will lead to peace whereas it leads to war. The history of the world dating back forty years prior to the great war in 1914 will bear out that statement. The following appears in the English Review for January, 1930:
The theory that armaments lead to war is not new; it was commonly used, in a slightly different form, by the opponents of compulsory training, who said that we were trying to instil "militarist" ideas into the youth of the nation. But is it easily disproved. In 1806 Prussia, which had universal service, easily defeated Austria, which had not. Austria, which up till then had had a great military reputation, was not too proud to learn from her enemy, and also introduced universal service; and about forty years later, on a vacancy occurring in the post which would normally carry with it the command in chief of the Austrian army in war, was forced to appoint an officer who had seen no active service at all. At that time the only Austrian officers who had ever been under fire were a few, quite juuior in rank, who had been in China at the time of the Boxer rising. "Militarism" in Austria meant unbroken peace from 1866 to 1914. But in 1870 France, which in the previous few years had rejected with derision the suggestion that she too should adopt the Prussian system, in turn found herself in opposition to Prussia; and the Paris mob shouted "A Berlin" with the enthusiam of irresponsible ignorance. After the disastrous war which followed, France also adopted universal service in an even more uncompromising fashion than either Prussia or Austria; and also remained at peace, except for some unimportant colonial campaigns, until 1914. From the material side of "armaments" as distinct from training, one is met by the rather serious difficulty of determining exactly what the word means. The League of Nations lately found itself in urgent need of a definition, for the purpose of dealing with the kindred questions which it calls the "traffic in arms" and the "private manufacture of arms." After long consideration it decided that a satisfactory definition was impossible, but that its purpose might be served by an enumeration of specific articles which any such definition would have bad to cover. The resulting list was long, and as nearly exhaustive as its compilers could make it; and it ended with swords, lances and bayonets.
We have a delegate at this peace conference in London, the Minister of National Defence, and he is not here to back up this resolution. I understand he has got sick and tired of things over there, and when he gets home he will probably decide that something will have to be done for this little fleet of ours. This fleet which hugs the shore and is afraid to go out to sea-'too proud to fight. If Colonel Ralston agrees to naval reduction and comes home to find the fleet he will have a hard time to find it.
He may find it down in the garage at Halifax. I am afraid somebody will steal it while the minister is over in London. If he does not. hurry home the hon. member for Southeast Grey will have our army abolished and only the Boy Scouts and the Girl Guides left.
In his opening remarks, instead of saying that we were united as an empire with New Zealand and Australia, Colonel Ralston spoke of nothing but status. It woidd have been far better had the delegates stayed at home. I see the minister's picture in monthly magazines over the statement that he is the glass of fashion. I have seen .the pictures of the minister inspecting different troops and one can see that he is really that, and perhaps he will bring back some new ideas along that line. But that is where his usefulness will end.
The Minister of Justice carries on the ory "down with war." The fact (that we have peace to-day is due to the efforts of the Canadian expeditionary forces, it is due to that great man Nelson who saved our empire in days gone by. All this talk about status does not mean a thing. A few years ago a Canadian missionary and his wife and son were carried off by Chinese brigands. The Canadian government were helpless in this matter, they had no power to act. What about this Geneva humbug, all this talk about status as a separate nation? All Ottawa could do was to turn to the British government and after firm representations were made by that government the prisoners were released and the delinquents punished. Germany wanted to belong to the League of Nations. Mussolini of Italy calls it a lot of horseplay, and one result of the peace parley over in England is that it has got France and Italy, two former fast allies, quarrelling over the parity of naval armament. If we could get ten years of silence from these pacifists, there would be some chance of having some peace, but we shall not as long as we have these peace pacts, agreements, excursions and pleasure trips going on at the expense of the people of Canada. The Canadian share of the expenses of the league is a large amount per capita. I believe more could be accomplished by Canada joining the national hockey league or the United States baseball league than the League of Nations. It is just a game of hide-and-go-seek, a nice easy trip across the sea for some of our worn-out politicians.
What did the former prime minister of South Africa, the present leader of the opposition, General Smuts, have to say about the peace parley? He emphasized in his speeches throughout Canada that we should

International Peace-Mr. Church
hear no more about equality of status, and that the time had arrived to seek to give some kind of substance and meaning to the unity of 'the empire and to help solve concrete empire problems such as trade, migration or defence.
Canada was represented over in England at the last anniversary of the battle of Trafalgar, and I notice the Morning Post had a leading editorial in that connection. Referring specially to Canada, that great newspaper says:
The anniversary of the Battle of Trafalgar yesterday serves as the peg on which the Morning Post to-day hangs its leading editorial on "Naval Necessities." Referring especially to Canada, the newspaper said: "Canada owes both her existence and her liberties in the first place to the Royal Navy, and then to that balance of power which maintains the British Empire in the new world as in the old. Let that balance be destroyed and how long, despite all pacts and treaties, would any part of that Empire rest secure?
"Canada is growing mightily, not only in industry and agriculture, but in commerce. Her ships are even now bringing to her people the fruits, sugar and other tropical commodities of the West Indies. For the protection of that traffic her naval provision of two destroyers is almost ludicrously inadequate. Her vast grain trade, her sea carriage east, west and south- these owe their security to the existence of the Royal Navy under whose benignant shade Canada has grown and prospered.
"These things are taken so much as a matter of course as to be ignored in the outlook of most of the Dominions. Yet it remains true that the trade of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have no other security than the fleet which they seldom see, but of which the very existence is a perpetual restraint to any potential enemy. The ideal of peace in an unarmed world is not served by ignoring the truth."
Last year when this resolution was before the house, I was quoting from English Review, that great imperialistic magazine, published in London, England, which is at last bringing England around to her senses regarding the danger that confronts the empire in this peace parley. France has practically retired from the parley. Italy, according to her prime minister, is going to expand or explode. There is going to be no parity between Italy and France. The whole trouble between Italy and France is that those fast allies, who did so much to win the war, have been placed in a position of fighting each other more or less in the press and outside the press, and dear knows what is going on behind closed doors. Bernard Shaw has described the scene in the League of Nations as "where they fight like blazes", something like what happened in the cabinet here a few years ago. In the English Review there is an article called War and the 
Man in the Street, and it refers to the situation prior to the war as follows:
The years 1909 to 1914 were full of political excitement; including the "militant" women's suffrage movement, a number of strikes in vital industries, the long Home Rule struggle, the death of King Edward, the passing of the Parliament Act, 1911. the Curragh incident, and the formation of the Ulster volunteers, for the purpose of forcible resistance to any project of putting Ulster under the control of Southern Ireland. Germany was, not unnaturally, deceived into thinking that this country, apart from its military weakness, would be debarred by its domestic troubles from taking any part in a continental war; and although the German fleet was by no means ready to tackle the British fleet unless it could effect a surprise, the German government made the Serajevo murders, in June 1914, the excuse for a war on which they had definitely decided at least three months before.
If the British fleet had not been mobilized and ready for action in August, 1914, dear knows what would have happened to the empire. The territorial army was also broken up. The English Review summarizes what took place, and then continues:
It can hardly be asserted, in face of the well-known facts here summarized, that we were prepared for war in 1914; but the fact that the war came has been freely U6ed as an argument to prove that the old maxim "si vis pacem para bellum" is a fallacy. It has become a political commonplace that armaments lead to war, whereas for over forty years the main factor which kept the Great Powers at peace was the size of their armies and the fear of the effect of the untried inventions with which they were equipped. The disarmament fallacy is even embodied in Art. 8 of the Covenant of the League of Nations; and for nine years the league has been vainly trying to find some means by which disarmament can be brought about. The Central Powers were theoretically disarmed by the peace treaties; we, whose military unpreparedness was, if not the actual cause of the late war, at any rate the principal cause of its long duration, have not only reduced our army to a lower figure than in 1914, but have taken the first step towards making a^ present of our vital naval supremacy to the United States. France is accused of "militarism" because she will not reduce her army below a size adequate to protect her against the enemy who has ravaged her territory twice within living memory. And in the same sacred cause of "disarmament and peace", we are being asked to agree to an arrangement under which the United States shall increase her navy until it is equal on paper to our own.
I think the country has had pretty nearly enough of these quack remedies for the elimination of war and for disarmament. It is further taken up in Geneva, where the parrot cry is invented: "Arbitration, security, disarmament." These high-sounding words are used. The English Review goes on:
His elected representatives have this year agreed to the compulsory arbitration of a lim-

International Peace-Mr. Church
ited class of international disputes by a court which has no power to enforce its judgments; before that he had been made responsible for securing the peace of western Europe by an undertaking to make war on an "agrcssor" state; and he is in process of being deprived of that naval superiority which alone could enable him to discharge that responsibility, except by the kind permission of the United States, which has undertaken no corresponding obligation. Added to this he is being told that it took more real courage to be a conscientious objector than to fight, and at the same time being deliberately dieted on books and plays which do not merely go to the opposite extreme from pre-war literature in emphasizing the horrors of war, but actually seem to deny its redeeming qualities of heroism and sacrifice.
The position in which the world finds itself to-day after the great war of 1914-18 is similar to what happened after the Napoleonic war of 1814-15. George Canning, as foreign secretary from 1823 to 1827, under the passive premiership of Lord Liverpool, was responsible for the foreign policy of his country in circumstances resembling with extraordinary exactness those of this decade. To Canning, as to his successor to-day, fell the task of liquidating the continental commitments which were inherited from a great European war, and of defining England's relations with the United States. Substituting France for Germany, the settlement of 1815 found Europe ranged against the defeated power under the banner of the Holy Alliance, consisting of Russia, Austria and Prussia, whose sovereigns pledged themselves, in a manner strangely similar to the allied powers who dominated the first council of the League of Nations, to regulate their foreign policy by the precepts of Christianity and to maintain peace. England, under Castlereagh's guidance, maintained with the Holy Alliance a friendly if informal association, much as Sir Austen Chamberlain was used to do in regard to our late allies of the war of 1914-18.
George Canning was faced with the same conferences. For ten years there was nothing but conferences that shouted for peace. The same men in every state who had brought about the European war had caused the peace parley too. I quote again from the Review:
No single formula can solve the problems of all nations which have their roots in wide differences of character, history and tradition. In politics the realist who can be right always must always defeat the idealist, who is bound to be wrong half the time, yet runs the risk, in his endeavour to meet all the circumstances of every case, of never being right. Further, Canning realized that, for a government with a real will of its own, participation in international congresses is a hollow sham, while a government without a real will must inevitably play second fiddle. England in 1825 could not afford to play second fiddle in the bankrupt orchestra of Europe. It was in these circumstances that Canning cut adrift from the Holy Alliance, and championed South American independence against the technical assertion of Spanish sovereignty and the practical challenge of the ambitions of the United States.
To-day we are faced with a situation more perilous than that which faced Canning. The hand of the doctrinaire is heavy over Europe. Africa and Asia have caught the infection, and the United States of America, to-day, as in 1825, friendly and pacific in her ultimate intentions, is dismayed at the European chaos and is seeking by every diplomatic means to restrict European influence outside Europe and to gather to herself the fruits of our pedantic follies. What are we doing? Instead of governing ourselves we are indulging, like the Holy Alliance, in an orgy of irresolute interference with other people's affairs. "Too quick for thought, for action too refined," we seek in the new sport of "finding a formula" a cure for ills threatening not merely a change in the relative power of different European nations, but a catastrophic decline in the power of each and all.
I am opposed to this resolution. There is no reason why this house, in view of what is happening to-day, should adopt this resolution; it would make the country appear ridiculous. Navies are still needed' in the world. Lord Lloyd, recently high commissioner in Egypt, who was the principal speaker at the navy league's Trafalgar day dinner in London on October 21 last, declared that he would settle the disarmament question by saying to the United States: "You build what you will, and let us build what we will." He added that the only peace of any use was the peace coming through security. He continued:
"We need to be careful amid press captions and the blare of Atlantic loudspeakers and keep our head," he continued, adding that the mere reduction of navies bore no relation to peace.
Referring to the crowds seen gathered about the Nelson Monument in Trafalgar Square today Admiral Sir Sidney Fremantle said he wondered whether the nation realized the great danger to itself "of stereotyping its naval policy to conform to the will of another country."
The gathering enthusiastically applauded bis assertion that "if the United States vTants a great navy, that is her affair, not ours. The strength of the British Navy is an affair of the British Empire and the British Empire alone. In the final analysis, freedom of action should be reserved for ourselves as our needs differ materially from those of every other nation."
The British Empire, Mr. Speaker, cannot exist without the sea and sea power. When we debated this resolution last year I quoted from the English Review, of November, 1928, as follows:
The voice of the peaeemonger resounds today over continents, to a never-ceasing accompaniment of treaties and undertakings, but we are drifting toward war. How easy it would be if we could simply scrap our armaments, sign a few more pacts, and preserve that peace which is the only serious political interest of all decent and Christian men. Instead, we mu6t
344	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Church
do our duty, and face naked facts. We are approaching the tenth anniversary of the armistice, and of a genuine and lasting peace there are no signs. The practice of open diplomacy and the august patronage bestowed on international intercourse by the league of Nations and Mr. Kellogg have created an atmosphere of open and public suspicion more alarming even than in the years immediately preceding 1914. Apostles of the new methods can ingeminate peace as much as they like, but they cannot shirk their terrible responsibility before the bar of history for the disastrous practical consequences of their ten years' experiment.
The resolution of the hon. member is not correct even as to its facts. It says that Canada is spending money for war, when we are not spending anything, because we have practically no army, and no navy. We are sponging all the time on the mother country to keep our trade routes open, and, in time of war, to protect our shores. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, in the absence of our first lord of the admiralty, who is at the disarmament conference, and in the absence of our commander in chief of the army, which my hon. friend from Southeast Grey wants to be demobilized1, and which I claim is demobilized already, except for boy scouts and girl guides, I think that this resolution might very well stand until our first lord returns and we find out what he is doing. It is all very well to have your picture taken and be seen in the fashion parade. I looked in the Bystander and the Sphere recently and Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like our delegate at the peace conference. If the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) wants to do something, let him bring Mr. Hoover and Mr. Ramsay MacDonald together to devise some way of disarming Chicago. It would be best to start off with something easy.
Russia, the black sheep of the allies, is mobilizing to-day. She is going to destroy Christianity, and we are the only nation that has not. sent a single note of protest to Soviet Russia against her persecution. Russia is mobilizing hundreds of thousands of men, marching towards China in battle array, with airplanes, tanks and every kind of modern military equipment. The Balkans to-day do not belong to the League of Nations. The two countries who suffered most in the war were France and England. I warn hon. gentlemen that any pacifist measures will have to be paid for a little later on, just like you paid up in 1914. Germany to-day is one of the most prosperous countries in the world.
I quote from the English Review of January, 1930:

At the peace conference France, as the greatest sufferer by the war, sought to disarm her old enemy Germany. Conscious of her fiasco in 1808, when her attempts to disarm Prussia led directly to the creation of the German army as it was in 1870 and 1914, she secured a paper limitation of the German army to 100,000 men, voluntarily recruited for long service; hoping thereby to prevent the building u.p of a trained reserve of the whole German nation. But the actual result is that Germany now has a highly trained nucleus of potential officers and N.C.O's, which could be expanded into a national army in a few months at the outside.
Germany, following her accustomed methods, is now working for a limitation of the French army which would leave her relatively as strong as, or stronger than, in 1914. If she gains her point, she will be in a better strategic position than ever; should she attack France again, she will be free of the Franeo-Russian alliance; and we, having handed over the command of the sea to America, shall be unable to prevent American supplies reaching Germany. Our expeditionary force has been cut down to the vanishing point, and the territorial army, though better in many respects than in 1914, is numerically weaker, and less than ever fitted to undertake the quick expansion which would be called for on mobilization. Helpless alike on land and at sea, we shall be compelled to \vait (incidentally disregarding our Locarno obligations) until Germany (and possibly Austria) has overcome France (and possibly Italy), and is prepared to do with us what she vainly hoped to do in 1914.
I am quoting from an article entitled War and the Man in the Street, written by one of the greatest military experts in the world, W. G. Carlton Hall. It appears in the January number of the English Review. To-day nobody in Germany is out of work, and the German government could in two or three months mobilize an army of millions right on the French border. The peace pact has succeeded, aided by the American delegates, in placing France and Italy, the loyal allies of the mother country in the late war, against each other. That is one of the tragedies of this peace parley.
The people of Ontario are contributing towards the cadet movement. They are taxed for cadet uniforms, and they are prepared to continue that help and to make larger votes every year. The cadet movement is not a military movement. Only half a million dollars was spent by the parliament of Canada last year, very largely for training camps to give the boys a holiday. Many of these boys are undernourished, and the training camps take them off the city streets, where their lives are imperilled by the hit and run motorists, and give them a holiday under the best possible conditions. For these and other reasons I hope the resolution will not pass.
march 6,1930	345
International Peace-Mr. Woodsworth
As I say, if we could have five or ten years of silence from the pacifists there would be some hope of perpetual peace. But so long as we are going to have peace conferences, peace pacts, and peace agreements, we are just as near to war as we were in, 1914.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is very little that need be added to what has been so well said by the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail), but I desire to associate myself with the motion which she has brought forward, particularly because of what underlies the motion, namely, the necessity in some way of definitely preparing for peace. I suppose we will all admit that the causes of modern wars are chiefly economic. So long as we have economic rivalry between groups and nations and empires, we shall have war. That is why some of us would like to see a change in the entire economic system. We cannot see how, short of that, we are going to have permanent peace; as long as there is the present struggle for markets one nation is bound to come into conflict with another. But I would not sa3r that this is the only cause. We have armaments themselves, and, as was so well said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) last year, as long as men have guns and ships nations will fight, and it seems to me to be highly desirable that we should do all in our power to lessen armaments in order that there shall be less provocation on the part of nation? to engage in war. And, as far as some of us are concerned, we think that Canada stands in a very good position indeed to take the lead along this line.
We have heard armaments advocated on the floor of this house as an insurance against war. I do not think, however, that in the past armaments have proved to be an insurance against war. Some of us, on the other hand, would advocate expenditures of the character proposed by the member for Southeast Grey, on the ground that they may very well be a real insurance against war. Undoubtedly, when war is imminent, the nations exploit to the limit the prejudices of their peoples. As long as peoples are ignorant of one another, as long as peoples are prejudiced against one another, we need to have a considerable measure of education. If the attitude of the member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) who preceded me, is at all common in the city of Toronto, it is very clearly an indication that some education along peace lines is necessary in that city. I am not quite sure that the proposed amount of S200,000 would be sufficient to accomplish the task, but I would say that we all to a greater dr less extent inherit these national prejudices, and it is difficult to overcome them.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, we should recognize that, since we are commited to the principles of peace, we have to prepare the people for an understanding of what peace involves. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was very happy in the earlier part of his speech; I do not think he was quite so happy, however, when he came to the middle of it and endeavoured to defend the British North America Act and its application in this regard. It seemed to me that that defence was a very laboured one indeed. He suggested that if the Dominion government should create a fund available for the establishment of professorships. or scholarships, in universities, in some way or another the Dominion government would be infringing on the rights of the provinces. As a matter of fact, the French government has established scholarships for young Canadians which will enable them to spend a period of study in Paris. I do not think anyone would say that the French government is infringing on the sovereignty of Canada by offering scholarships to young Canadians.

subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext: What about the Rhodes scholarships?

subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Yes, the Rhodes
scholarships, if you like, as suggested by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). Mr. Cecil Rhodes, a great imperialist, has through his scholarship for years, infringed, if you like, upon our sovereignty, and upon that of the United States, and yet large numbers of our universities have been very glad to avail themselves of the possibility of sending young students abroad. I think that the argument of the Minister of Justice was very far-fetched indeed. If the provinces objected to having any chair endowed in their universities surely that argument does not apply in the case of offering scholarships to some of our students to go abroad. Undoubtedly a fund could be provided under an independent commission by which young men or young women who are anxious to qualify for foreign service in the days to come could avail themselves of the opportunities to travel abroad and of coming into contact with other people.
As soon as we come to certain particular questions there are some in this house who
International Peace-Mr. COMMONS
Woodsworth
are very solicitous lest the British North America Act be infringed upon. For example, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when in British Columbia last year was asked by a deputation there whether he would be willing to have the Kellogg pact framed and put in the schools of the Dominion, or in the schools of that province. The Prime Minister, perhaps quite properly, said, yes, he would be delighted to have the Kellogg pact framed and put on the school walls, but it had to be with the consent of the schools. He was very careful in that. But I ask you, what is done in the case of the cadet services? We are spending half a million dollars in cadet services, and officers, paid by this government, are urging those cadet services very often upon an unwilling public. Again and again I have protested on this floor against the cadet services being promoted in such a fashion. We have tried to cut down the expenditure upon cadet services. We have had the assurance from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) that his officers would not be allowed to take the initiative in permitting this kind of thing in our public schools; yet they are continuing to do so. I read, for example, a letter that came only the other day to the Winnipeg public school board:
Winnipeg, Man., February 5, 1930.
Mr. F. A. All den,
Secretary, School Board,
Winnipeg.
Dear Sir:
May permission be granted for a deputation of citizens to wait upon the school board on Thursday evening, February 6, when the management committee of that organization will be in session?
The delegation will deal with the introduction of cadet training in the schools and there will be at least five who wish to address the board on this important matter.
Yours very truly,
(Signed) Geo. H. Gillespie, Lt. Col.
Here you have a lieutenant colonel who, if I understand aright, is in the employ of a department of this government, pressing cadet services upon the schools of my own city, which has not had cadet sendees, which hitherto has refused to have them and which I think, will continue so to refuse. Yet we are so very solicitous if it is proposed to establish in our provinces scholarships which would allow someone thus to have his own educational opportunities enlarged. I believe the Minister of Justice-and I wish he were here-has too much good clear French logic in his make-up to delude himself in regard to matters of that kind. I should expect the Minister of Justice to rise in his seat and protest against the way

in which the cadet services are being forced upon the provinces.
The Minister of Justice seemed to imply that by taking action along this line we would be breaking an agreement. I believe that is altogether too far-fetched. It seems to me to be more in keeping with the former part of his speech, if he, as one who undoubtedly has done a great deal for the promotion of peace, would undertake to map out some kind of program for the promotion of peaceful sentiments in this country, just as we hope other people will promote peaceful sentiments in their countries. Thus he would be doing a very good work indeed. The minister had to admit that, after all, Canada was spending only about $200,000 on the League of Nations and all the services connected therewith, and he seemed to think it was a matter for congratulation that already we had attained the objective set by the hon. member for Southeast Grey. I do not believe that is her objective. Even though $200,000 has been spent by this great Dominion of Canada in that fashion, practically $20,000,000 is being spent in connection with our defence department. No; the minister was on sounder ground when he spoke about the development of international machinery and of an international conscience.
The point is that this internationalism does not develop altogether by itself. If we want to accomplish anything we organize in order to do so; we set up certain types of machinery; we try to encourage certain ways of thinking, and I do not think we are doing our full duty in this country if we simply send certain delegates to the League of Nations once a year, who may come back and make a few speeches afterwards, while we leave the great part of our population without any adequate knowledge of international affairs or of the new world that is so rapidly developing round about us, and which is bound to bring us in touch with events of the utmost importance.
