subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice in replying to the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mae-phail) said that the underlying principle of the resolution was the promotion of peace. I think he might have gone a little further; as I interpret it the underlying motive of the resolution is the promotion of peace by education. I think that addition is very significant, because there is no effective promotion of peace except by education.
I think it a tragic aspect of our peace efforts that we try almost every other expedient but this. I will mention one or two of the methods which are being employed, not to disparage them at all, because we welcome every effort to establish peace, but in order to show that there are certain methods which are limited by their inherent character. Let us take, for instance, tihe establishment of arbitration and judicial procedure. That is good, and we commend the government for having signed the optional clause on behalf of Canada. That is all to the good, but I think we should note the limitations of this kind of effort on behalf of peace. The machinery of law, no matter how new or how bright and shining, will not operate unless it is backed up by an enlightened public opinion. In the country to our south we note that the eighteenth amendment, which is a law in the constitution of one of the greatest commonwealths in the world, has behind it one of the most elaborate and efficient pieces of judicial machinery of which we can conceive, but we know that that machinery has been largely inoperative because public opinion has not been educated up to the point of supporting it through thick and thin. I am not going to argue the merits of the eighteenth amendment; I am giving it just as an analogy.
Then I think I could come nearer home. I could refer to some laws which have been passed in our provinces and which have had beihind them the very efficient system of law which we are proud to think we possess in Canada, yet these laws and prohibitions have been absolutely ineffective simply because public opinion has not been enlightened to the proper point. So arbitration, and the settlement of difficulties by judicial procedure, although they mark a big advance, will prove -I hope I shall not be thought to be posing as a prophet when I say this-to be tragically inadequate, if in tihe participating countries there is not an enlightened public opinion to
uphold the judges who sit upon that august body. This winter I heard the present chief justice of the Limited States explain the machinery of the international court. The one thing which interested me was the very excellent expedient for getting a sound judgment upon all questions which came before the court, and that was that each judge had to sit up at night and write out his own judgment before he collaborated with his brother judges in the final decision. That would be a splendid thing for all judicial bodies, and it might be a good thing for committees of parliament. This is a splendid machine; it is modern; it is up to date; it is calculated to give a sound judgment, but if enlightened public opinion is not fully behind it, that splendid machinery will not operate in the manner intended.
There is another expedient, that of disarmament. I need only mention this to prove that the weakness of our efforts for peace lie in the absence of a strong, enlightened public opinion. Why are all our disarmament conferences fiascos, why is it that the meetings of our wisest counsellors are of no avail? It is because they are not sure of the public opinion which lies behind them in their respective countries. They are paralyzed in their peace efforts by fear, by psychological conditions at home, and fear is the twin sister of ignorance. We could save time and expense, and we would be wise to do it, by refusing to enter into these conferences until the psychological conditions of the various countries had so improved that there would be a practical basis upon which the counsellors of the world could get together. A man does not require to be very wise to lay his finger upon the cause of the failure of our disarmament conferences. It is quite easy for Canada to say that France is not sincere, that Italy is not sincere, but are we sincere?
We talk lightly about cadet training, but I remember reading in the proceedings of the sixth preparatory disarmament conference of an objection made by the representative from Poland. The matter under discussion concerned the reduction of European reserves and Poland objected to any reduction until countries such as Canada, the United States and England considered a reduction in the number of their cadets. This objection puts cadet training upon a different plane of argument, and so long as we in Canada foster this insidious form of militarism we retard international understanding.
There is another matter in which I think we ought to prove our sincerity, and that is in regard to our air service. If we were sincere we would divorce our air service from our
348	. COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Bird
military department. Someone says that it has been done, and if so I think it is more than a matter of commendable domestic policy; it is a matter of international wisdom.
As the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) suggested this afternoon, we should undertake a campaign of debunking history as it is taught to the rising generation in Canada. We should enter the moving picture theatre and do some expurgating there. The other night I visited a theatre where an American film was being shown, and as far as I could see, the only motive of the picture was to make prohibition unpopular and militarism popular. Not only should we expurgate our moving picture shows, but there are other shows which should be treated in the same manner. I attended at the bar of the Senate when this parliament was opened, and there saw the representative of the crown surrounded by a tremendous military show. I have asked this question of myself over and over again, why should a country like Canada, with pacific intentions and a peaceful disposition, permit this annual function to be disfigured by the protrusion of militarism? If we are sincere and want to make the mental environment of our children such as will develop a pacific attitude in life, let us see to it that as far as we are able they are saved from this militaristic show which is a relic of pre-war days.
Although we may change our mental environment, there remains an attitude of mind which, unfortunately, we are all bom with, not because we are imbued with any militaristic ideas but because we are born human. I agree with Professor William James, the great psychologist, when he says that pacificists make a crucial mistake in their opposition to militarism when they overlook the natural combative instincts of men. That inr stinct cannot be overlooked. You may do away with cadets, you may expurgate our histories from all allusion to war, you may transform our environment entirely, but you cannot eradicate the impulses which have come down to us from time immemorial and which rest securely in the breasts of the mildest of men. These impulses must be taken into consideration because every now and again humanity will break out in a form of madness. After all, it is not the military leaders, it is not the misguided politicians who make war, it is the surging mania of the people themselves. How can we deal with these impulses which now and again run riot and deluge the world in blood? Only by education, only by taking the rising generation as early as you can and directing those impulses into constructive instead of destructive channels.

The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) has laid her finger on the whole secret, but the proper place to start is with the schools, the teachers, not the universities. That is where I differ from my hon. friend. I think she is not catching the rising generation soon enough. When persons get into a university, they are hopeless so far as change of ideas is concerned. You can inculcate new ideas only in the early years of life. I pity any young man or woman who enters a university with militaristic ideas, because there is in a university nothing that is calculated ever to modify such ideas. It is on the earlier years of life that you must depend for moulding the mind of the young Canadian in a pacific direction.
I do not think it is worth while anyway thinking about the universities. This has led the hon. member for Southeast Grey into difficulties with the hon. Minister of Justice in regard to provincial rights. I do not think it is worth while raising that question because I believe the government can reach the mind of young Canada without interfering with the universities. Even if the government was in control of the universities, I would not think it worth while tampering with them for the cause of peace, or, indeed, for any cause. But I think the government can find ways and means to reach the young mind of Canada with enlightened ideas as to our duty towards mankind.
It is not only international relationships that need enlightenment; it is our ideas of human nature in general. I can remember the time when I thought very differently of a German from what my boy does to-day. Nothing could be more diametrically opposed than my idea in my youth of a German to that which my son has in his youth. Neither is true; neither is just. When France was the enemy of England generations ago, an Englishman's idea of a Frenchman was a travesty and yet this very night we hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) eulogizing the clarity and precision of the French mind. If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had been born two generations earlier, he would not have looked upon the Frenchman in that light at all; he would have said that the Frenchman is the most frivolous animal on earth.
I have heard that our universities to-day teach that European humanity is divided into Nordics and Mediterraneans. If a university professor teaches that Europe is divided into a superior and an inferior race in each of which temperaments are fundamentally different, what is the use of the hon. member for Southeast Grey trying to enlist the help of the

International Peace-Mr. Irvine
universities? Our universities themselves are tinged with racial prejudice. They hold ideas of humanity that are not worthy even of a high school intelligence. So let us forget the universities. Let the present government, and every government for that matter, try to instil into the mind of the rising generation just ideas, true ideas, about other nations.
What about international relationships? If there had been some means of enlightening the people of the world on international relationships prior to 1914, there would have been no war. I will go further and say that if the foreign offices of the governments of Europe had been enlightened on foreign affairs, there would have been no war. You cannot conceive of an ignorance deeper than that which infested the mind of Lord Grey prior to 1914. Here was a minister of foreign affairs in the British government who did not know the history of his own department, who for years had acquiesced in a secret understanding with France and who, at the outbreak of war, did not know the details of its history. Surely we want some agency set up, whereby not only common men and women but foreign secretaries and even prime ministers and cabinets may be enlightened. There never before was any political ignorance so great in its dimensions, so tragic in its potentialities, as that which reigned supreme in the minds of politicians in Europe in 1914.
So the hon. member for Southeast Grey should not have to plead with the house to establish ways and means whereby we can penetrate this great darkness which is the breeding place of hatreds, which is full of possibilities that we hardly dare think about. The hon. member for Southeast Grey has been like a voice crying in the wilderness for a year or two on this proposition, and I was somewhat sorry to hear the reply of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) although it is not difficult to recognize that the minister has his bright spots, his idealisms. I do not think he ever speaks on a question of this kind that he does not disarm one's come-back by revealing his comprehension and sympathy. But I want to ask him: How are we going to make this principle operative unless we somehow or another deal broadly with this matter of provincial rights? I admit we are a confederation and that provincial rights are sacred. Because they are sacred, do not put them in the way of progress. The fact that they are sacred is a reason not to put them there. When the Chinese saw the first locomotive coming along, they put their sacred dishes on the track. It was because they were sacred that they should not have put them there. So our provincial rights which
are sacred and without which there could not be Canada, must be safeguarded by keeping them out of the way of progress that must not be delayed. Parliament has the supreme duty of proving to the world that Canada has, not a number of little souls, but one big soul, this unitary thing which is not a matter of materials but which is a spirit, a soul. When the Minister of Justice or anyone else goes to the League of Nations, he must 'be backed up, not by a collection of little, uncertain, opposed souls, but by one big, agreed, enlightened and convinced soul, and only in that way can Canada take her place in the councils of the world.

subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
In some respects the motion before the house is highly commendable. It at least presupposes the possibility of peace. It suggests, and in itself assists, the development by peaceful methods of a will favourable to peace. It indicates the value of education to the future peace of mankind. It specifically asks that we begin an educational program for peace. In all these respects the resolution might well be welcomed by this house, and I am sure that the people of Canada generally will feel very grateful to the lady member of the house for having brought this matter to the attention of parliament, and for having devoted so much of her time and energy to a study of this question and to the promotion of her ideals of peace.
If this resolution comes to a vote, I shall vote for it more perhaps because of its implications than for its specific recommendations. I had a good deal of sympathy with the attitude of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this afternoon. I admit that this talk of provincial rights about which we hear so much does get a little tiresome at times, and very often we could wish that it was out of the way. Nevertheless the address of the Minister of Justice this afternoon was a delight to me at least, and I was particularly pleased with its spirit and, as a previous speaker, (Mr. Bird) has mentioned, with the sympathy which he manifested in regard to the main idea of the resolution. He summarized admirably some of the agencies for peace with which Canada is associated. First of all he drew our attention to the fact of which I presume we are all aware, that the influences of the last war are still working towards peace, in that the suffering and destruction and futility of it has left its mark upon the imagination of the people. That is true. Of course, we are also aware of the fact that these influences pass away with the generations, and therefore we cannot rely upon them-I am not suggesting that the min-

International Peace-Mr. Irvine
ister implied that we could-as a lasting influence. He also mentioned the League of Nations and the efforts that are being put forward by labour nationally and internationally; the signing of the Kellogg pact; the disarmament conference in Great Britain at which we are represented; and our signing of the optional clause. Then he made reference to what is perhaps of even greater significance, and that is the development of what he called an international conscience. All these agencies, and numerous others, both of an economic and commercial significance, to which the minister did not refer, are all working, I believe, towards peace. The time will come when it will be clear that the world is in fact an economic unit, and what is more important, that the world is a human unit, and as these ideas bear in upon the imagination of the world they will help forward the cause of peace in every department of human affairs.
The Minister of Justice found that it would not perhaps be wise for this government and parliament to appear to be interfering with an educational question since jurisdiction in education is left to the provinces. That consideration has to be met. I agree with the argument of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that we have got around that difficulty in respect to such matters as cadet training and other subjects, and it may be possible for us to get around that difficulty here. As the minister has such a splendid conception of what is happening in the world to-day in regard to peace, and as he is so manifestly sympathetic to the idea, I hope that he will not allow the splendid sentiments which he has expressed to go to seed without yielding some results. If he finds that any part of the constitution stands in the way, let him alter it or find some way to get around it, and I can assure him that he will have a great deal of support in his efforts in that regard.
Let me turn now more particularly to the resolution. I think I may consider myself free to speak critically of what it asks for, inasmuch as the hon. mover herself has indicated that she is not quite satisfied with its terminology The resolution asks, in the first place, that at least one dollar be expended for peace for eveiy one hundred dollars that is expended in preparation for war. As far as I am concerned, that is not enough. She might very properly reply: that is better than nothing. I agree, but the point I want to make without further argument is that I do not think our peace efforts should be conditioned upon or limited in any way by the extent to which we engage in war preparations. I think that

should be a thing entirely by itself. Of course, the logic of the resolution is unanswerable. The lady member may very well argue that if we are, as we declare, a peace-loving people, it is not too much to ask that we spend one dollar for peace for every hundred that we spend in preparing for war.
My next objection to the resolution is that a nation educated not to fight will still fight as readily as a nation which is educated to fight, if and when the conditions of war obtain. I know that my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Bird) will not agree with me there. I can imagine, however, an educated man, as highly educated a man as my hon. friend from Nelson, being quite willing to put up a real fight under certain circumstanoes. He might know that it was quite foolish to fight, that it would not help him at all even if he won, but still I believe he would say that there are times and conditions when he would rather stand up and be defeated than allow himself to be trampled on by anybody.

I knew that he was the very type of Englishman who would take that fighting attitude. Education in the academic sense in which education cannot stop war is used in this resolution-if you mean education in its broadest sense, the use of every avenue that leads to the mind, and sometimes perhaps to the stomach, of mankind, I might alter my opinion-I can imagine that some of the most highly educated professors would probably be the leaders in our militaristic strategy.
I have another slight objection to the specific demands of the resolution, and that is that a thorough understanding of international affairs would probably make a militarist out of our peace student. If he were really in touch with all the practical international questions of Europe-we need not confine ourselves to Europe, but say international affairs generally-he would have to deal with such practical questions as the present political unrest in India; he would have to deal with the . practical questions which are agitating the governments of Italy and France; he would have to deal with a thousand practical questions that neither you nor I have ever heard of, and I am just afraid he might come away with the idea that we had better be prepared for war as quickly as possible. I am afraid of professors of that type. I well remember a professor who spoke very highly of a certain financial reform, who declared in private to small groups of people his aversion to the monopoly of banks and all that sort of thing.

International Peace-Mr. Spencer
But when that professor was called to give evidence before our committee on banking all those opinions vanished, and he then became the champion of high finance. Strange thing! I would be afraid of an educated professor doing something like that.
Let me say next that so far as I am concerned the universities would be the last place in which to expect the beginning of so desirable a human achievement as peace. I know of no instance in world history-there may be one-when any great human movement took its rise in the universities. I think it is more probable that the universities would oppose it. I have more faith in public schools than in universities, and I have more faith in the ordinary groups of people who meet together and face their own problems than I have in the universities. I think that the organizations of the people of Canada that we are witnessing about us to-day, the labour organizations and the farmer organizations meeting in countless little groups all over the western provinces and in large rooms in our cities,- the usual meeting places of our labour people

these are the places where education of this sort will be disseminated. I have faith in that kind of education.
But my last point is this: who is going to prepare the course of peace study for the students in the universities? I have heard the hon. member for Southeast Grey criticize our public school text books, and I think rightly so. We ought to have some control over those text books, and yet we find that they are not what we want. We w'ould have much less control over a course of peace study in our universities. Who will select the professors, for instance, and who will direct them? Let us take as an example McGill university. The president is one of our most distinguished military leaders. Now, would he select the peace professor, and would he draft the course of study to be followed? I speak with all respect of that most distinguished military leader, and I am prepared to give to him all the honour that Canadians extend to him; but in connection with our discussion it is a fact that the president of McGill university is one of our outstanding generals. That is only one case; there may be many others. I do not think that the actual recommendations of the resolution will be the best way to carry out the idea which no doubt the hon. member for Southeast Grey had in mind. subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject under consideration is a very important one indeed, and our thanks are due to the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) for again bringing it before us. Of course there are many views in regard to this question, but in the main there are two schools of thought; on the one hand, those who believe that the best way to prepare for peace is to be ready for war; and on the other hand, those who think that by cutting down armaments we can preserve peace. Personally I do not think either school is right. If I had to choose between them I would prefer to accept the opinion of those who believe in disarmament because less harm would be done at the outbreak of war; and in my opinion war is inevitable while present economic world conditions continue.
What are the causes of war? In times gone by we had religious wars; I think those are a thing of the past. We have had territorial wars; I think they also are of the past. We have had wars brought about by national animosity; surely with our peace conferences and the various arbitration and peace treaties of the last two or three years we have got beyond that stage. Then why is it that everybody thinks that war is inevitable? It is because people realize that most wars originate in economic rivalry. And when we have found what is wrong in the economic sense, and taken the proper corrective measures, we shall have made war impossible by removing the cause. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we have not given sufficient study to the result of the mechanization of industry. To-day through that great revolution in industry, through the aid of science and invention, there

International Peace-Mr. Spencer
is no difficulty at all in producing greater and greater quantities of goods with less and less man power. In other words, we are rapidly transferring the load from the shoulders of mer, to machines. In doing this we are of course throwing more and more men out of employment. Even in Canada to-day we are up against a big problem of unemployment. This problem confronts the United States and Great Britain and most other countries of the world to a still greater extent. We have to recognize the fact that the payroll is the purchasing power of the people, and if you cut down the payroll of the people you simply increase the quantity of the goods on the shelves that cannot be sold. The problem of production has been solved; we now have before us the problem of consumption. What is the usual suggestion as a means of getting out of this dilemma? The most orthodox suggestion is to produce more, to consume less, and to export the surplus. To my mind that suggestion is absolutely absurd. According to my knowledge of economics, with all the money paid out in the cost of production it is impossible to buy back the goods in the figure of price. At least some economists go so far as to say that we do not spend more than sixty cents of the producer's dollar. If we have not the money to buy back the surplus goods we export, how are we to have the money to buy the goods that are imported in exchange for the goods sent out of the country? The biggest struggle in the world to-day is the effort made by all countries to find markets outside their own borders. In peace we have economic war; on the other hand it might well be said that " war is economic peace," because in peace times, with a curtailment of credit, you have not sufficient purchasing power to buy back the goods that are made. Credit is put in operation to produce more goods, but not to purchase goods, and therefore we are continually producing more and more goods for an already glutted market. It is this struggle of one country competing against another for similar markets that is creating the economic warfare. When war breaks out, as it unfortunately does now and again, we have economic peace, because then there is no such thing as a consumer's problem. War is the greatest consumer of goods in a given time, and so we find that in wartime everyone is pretty well off, everyone has money. Poverty is at its lowest ebb. If we do not have war, we have the accumulation of goods and increased unemployment. In the last hundred years we have advanced tremendously in the matter of industry; we 
have revolutionized the production of goods, but during that last hundred years we have carried on with an old credit system that was all right in the old days but which does not fit our conditions of to-day. As long as we stay with this policy of exchange that is out of date, then just so long shall we have before us the very serious problem of getting rid of the goods that are produced. Various suggestions have been made for the solving of this problem. Some suggest the elimination of armaments. That certainly would help to the extent that if war did break out fewer people would be killed in a given time; but if you take the people away from the making of goods, in the way of armaments, you increase more and more the number of unemployed. Another way to solve the problem is to get rid of people. Great Britain is doing her level best to migrate her people. The United States is doing her very best to keep people from coming into her country. The matter of birth control has also been suggested, and yet none of these seem to me to be a solution of the problem.
In supporting the amendment to the resolution placed before the house by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, I do so because I think we might, in that committee, secure certain information that would be useful to the house. But I agree with the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), that even if we do set up international scholarships, if the scholars are taught not along the lines of the newer economics but simply in accordance with the present methods of teaching- which, by the way, have brought us to this checkmate-then I say we would not be gaining our end. If we can ensure the teaching to the students of the newer economics, and if these students, with their ability, can go out into the world and preach those newer economics, they will be doing something to solve those questions which relate to the purchasing power of the people. The resolution is an excellent one and should be passed by the house.
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, I would say that peace is largely a matter of consumption. When we have solved the problem of consumption, made it possible for the people of the world to enjoy the goods of the world-which they are doing to-day only to a very small extent-we will get rid of the miseries of war and poverty and crime, and all those things that are detrimental to any nation, even to our own.

Mr. Speaker, I would not

International Peace-Mr. Mackenzie King
like the motion of my hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) to be allowed to pass or to be dropped without saying a word on it, because I find myself in entire agreement with her as to the several proposals suggested in her motion considered individually, though forced to disagree with her when asked to assent to them in combination. The motion breaking it into parts, reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, for every one hundred dollars spent for war one dollar should be spent to promote peace-
Taken by itself I imagine that the only fault to be found with this proposition would be the one mentioned by the last speaker, namely that the amount is anything but comparable to what it should be. However, my hon. friend's motion relates not simply to the amount to be paid for the promotion of peace, but to promotion of peace in a particular way. The motion goes on to suggest:
-by setting up a chair of international relationships and by instituting international scholarships in each Canadian university.
Here again, as I have said, I find myself in wholehearted accord with the object of the resolution in its separate propositions, considered separately. I think it would be an excellent thing to have a chair of international relationships-I will not say in every university but certainly in some of our universities -and, similarly, I feel that international scholarships in each Canadian university, or at least in some Canadian universities would have much to commend them. But I would want to be quite sure as to just what my hon. friend means by international scholarships. Perhaps I might say a word first of all in regard to international scholarships.
In a great many countries most of the universities have what are known as travelling scholarships or fellowships. I cannot conceive of any more useful form of benefaction than the founding of scholarships or the endowment of universities with chairs on different subjects, but from the resolution I really do not know whether what my hon. friend has in mind is a scholarship to be given to Canadians to study at foreign universities or a scholarship to be given to foreigners to study in Canadian universities.
