Well, if that
is the case I rather sympathize with both, but I do feel that scholarships, seeing that they have to do with educational institutions, should be founded by individuals or societies or by provincial governments rather than by the federal government. Similarly with regard 2419-23
to a chair of international relations; I think before asking any government to vote public money for the purpose we would have to define rather carefully what is to be included in the work of instruction on international relations. International relations is a very large subject. It embraces many matters, some of them differing widely in character from others. May I suggest just one topic which I think would appropriately and necessarily come within the scope of instruction of a chair of international relations, that is, the subject of the tariff. The tariff has a very important bearing on many matters not far removed from questions of peace and war. I would want to know whether the chair of international relations to be established by this government would include instruction on the tariff, and if it would I should like to be pretty sure as to the particular government which would control the money for the purpose. Let us assume for a moment that a chair of international relations was to be established at the University of Toronto. That university is a provincial institution. I assume that the moment we agreed to appropriate a sum of money for the purpose we would be told by Mr. Ferguson of Toronto that he would very gladly accept the money we wished to hand him from the public treasury, but that he would claim the right to appoint the professor. Personally I would not care to have a son of mine trained on the subject of international relations by a professor who might be appointed by Mr. Ferguson for the purpose, and I am inclined to think my hon, friend might feel the same about any daughter of hers.
I mention these facts simply because, after all, they do illustrate some of the considerations which a ministry has to take into account in voting public money for educational purposes. I do not think it can be denied that the professorships and scholarships in universities are concerned primarily with matters of education; the words of themselves are sufficient to indicate that. I must say that I cannot see wherein we would be improving either international relations or internal relations, as far as our own country is concerned, if, as a federal government, we began to take up matters of education which up to the present time have been dealt with exclusively or have been largely dealt with, by the different provinces.
Now, as to spending public money for the purpose of promoting peace, I remember that when last year my hon. friend introduced a motion in somewhat similar terms I pointed out that practically all the expenditure of government is for the purposes of peace. I

354	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Mackenzie King
do not think it can be said that even the expenditures of the Department of National Defence are for the purposes of war. They are essentially expenditures for the purposes of preserving peace. However, allow that to pass and consider other branches of government. Surely everything that has to do with the Department of Justice relates to peace; peace is founded upon justice. Take next the Department of External Affairs; I think that department might very well foe termed the department of international relations, or the department of international conciliation, one might almost say, because I am quite certain the matters that are dealt with there are all dealt with in a manner which it is hoped will promote peace and good will among the different nations in their relations with this Dominion. As a matter of fact the whole work of that department, is an effort to deal with all international relations on a basis of reason rather than of force, and as I see it that is the distinction between peaceful and warlike methods. War relies upon force for achieving its ends, while the Department of External Affairs concerned with maintaining and promoting peace relies in international relations upon the appeal to reason. All the money that is being expended on the work of the Department of External Affairs does, I think, fall entirely within the category my hon. friend has in mind when she asks this parliament to vote money for the promotion of peace.
I am going to ask my hon. friend to allow me to suggest a form of educational work which very well might be advanced by the Department of External Affairs. It is educational in character but comes I think, within the scope of that department of the federal government rather than within the scope of the provincial Department of Education. The cooperation of both governments would be required to render it effective.	I refer
to the right kind of publicity to be given the Briand-Kellogg pact. Last fall when I was in western Canada I had the privilege of addressing an armistice day gathering at Ocean Falls, a small industrial community on the Pacific coast. It was one of the most impressive gatherings I have ever attended. A feature of the occasion was the unveiling of the Briand-Kellogg pact for the renunciation of war on the wall of the little church in which this meeting took place. This document had been suitably engrossed and framed and was hanging there, and the unveiling was the central feature of the Armistice day service. At that gathering I was reminded of a request which had come to the government asking that copies of this pact 
should be put in all the schools and churches of the dominion. I was so impressed by what I saw that day that I did not hesitate to say that I was quite sure a proposal of the kind would meet with the general approval of the members of this house, and that I intended when parliament met to ask for an appropriation for the distribution of the Briand-Kellogg pact in a form which would enable it to be hung in schools and churches, wherever they might wish to have it.
That, of course, would require the cooperation of educational authorities. I am happy to inform my hon. friends that since that statement was made I have received from the heads of the educational departments or the premiers of several of the provinces requests for copies of the pact for that very purpose. They have intimated that if the Department of External Affairs will supply them with these copies in a suitable form for hanging they will see that they are distributed and given a place in the schools of the province. That will cost a little money; even the printing, framing and distributing of these pacts will involve the expenditure of a considerable sum. As I see it, it is our duty rather than that of the provinces to ask for that expenditure; the publicity given an instrument of peace such as the Briand-Kellogg pact falls properly and appropriately within the work of the Department of External Affairs. I doubt very much if we could expect the educational authorities of the provinces to give us any money for the purpose of having the pact printed and distributed, but we are happy to be assured of their cooperation in giving it a place in the schools, where I think, its being publicly exhibited, will render a great service. That would be carrying out what I think is the fundamental idea of the motion of my hon. friend, namely, that something of an educational character should be carried on in connection with the work of the Department of External Affairs upon the all-important matter of the promotion of peace. If her resolution were to read, "that in the opinion of the house for every one hundred dollars spent for war one dollar should be spent to promote peace by distributing the Briand-Kellogg pact to be hung in the schools and churches of our country," and so forth, I could vote for that resolution without any question because I could feel that I was confining myself to an obligation which properly belonged to the federal government While I think the idea of establishing chairs of international relations and the granting of international scholarships is excellent, I differ

International Peace-Mr. Mackenzie King
from my bon. friend in believing that we should use our money for that purpose rather than for the purpose I have just described.
We need money more urgently for such work as is being carried on by the Department of External Affairs than the country needs at this particular time scholarships or chairs on international relations. The hon. member has said, and I think very wisely, that many of our young men should be trained to a certain extent in diplomacy, that they should have the opportunity of spending some time in the legations and some time in the Department of External Affairs. She mentioned that we have two legations, and I tried to have her say three, which I think she will admit is the correct number. We have legations in France, the United States and in Japan. We have an office at Geneva where Canada is represented by an advisory officer, and, in addition, we have the high commissioner's office in Great Britain which has to some extent to do with international affairs. AH these establishments are under the direction of the Department of External Affairs.
Experience has shown that there is a very close relationship between the universities and this department of government. The Department of External Affairs has to look to the universities for trained men to carry on its work, men who have obtained a high position in history, international law, political economy or political science in its different branches. The universities will in time be the better off by the addition to their staffs, particularly in the departments of history, international law, political science and government, of men who have had practical experience in our Department of External Affairs and in the legations. I believe that the object the hon. member has in view would be best obtained, and probably in time will be obtained in considerable measure by the return to the universities later on of some of those men who have left the universities, come for a time into the Department of External Affairs, who have become associated with one or more of the legations and gained in that way a practical knowledge of the working of government in international relations. Such men would return to the university faculties, either to the chairs of history, international law or political science in any of its branches, and would there undertake to lecture in a practical way on international relations. There have been many examples of outstanding men such as President Taft, the late President Wilson and others who after an association with government have returned to universities to deliver courses of 2419-23i
lectures on government, with a service infinitely more valuable to the student because they were able to speak as being of those who spoke with authority, having themselves gone through the mill and knowing from first hand experience what they were talking about.
If the motion of the hon. member were carried and we had to look around to-morrow for the professors to appoint, where would we get them? There is no school to-day which specifically trains men to fill chairs of inter-nationl relations, but there are men in our service who have been professors in universities, wiho have left those universities to enter the public service and who have thus rendered a great service to the country, who could return to-morrow to any university fully equipped to fill positions such as my hon. friend has mentioned. I do not know where else their equals could be found.
I believe this whole question would be made much clearer than I am able to make it if the suggestions made by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) were carried out and the amendment adopted and the resolution thereby permitted to go to the committee on international relations. I can see no possible harm, and I think a great deal of good might come through having this particular resolution referred to that committee. The committee could call before it a desired representative of universities and those members of the Department of External Affairs who have come from our universities and who have first hand knowledge of these matters. It will be found that there are in the department those who are possessed of a very intimate knowledge of what would be expected of a chair of international relations. The members of the committee could also ascertain for themselves whether or not the carrying out of what my hon. friend has in mind along the line I have suggested this evening might not prove to be more in accord with what she herself hopes to accomplish, than the resolution as at present worded.
I shall be very happy to vote for the amendment in order to allow the resolution to go to the committee for that purpose.

subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) on her return to the house, to the benefit of all? I agree largely with everything she has said, and especially with the first sentence of her remarks of yesterday, that her motion perhaps might have been worded otherwise. On a previous occasion the hon. member referred to the improvement in her temper due to the re-
356	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
moval of her tonsils; might I suggest that perhaps the motion was written before the operation, and the speech made after?
The motion is rather involved and, as the Prime Minister has suggested, it opens the door to divergent views. 1 am not accustomed to walking a.t once right and left, therefore I do not feel quite comfortable in accepting the motion as it is. I am in agreement with the Prime Minister as to the acceptance of the amendment of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), because it will help in clearing up these little difficulties. This resolution would be put in the hands of the committee, and that committee could call some of the members of the Department of External Affairs and other people who might throw some light upon the question.
It seems to me that we should never connect too intimately the very broad question of the development of our international relationship, and the education of our people in that direction, with the question of peace or war. I entirely sympathize with the endeavours of most of my progressive friends, on the other side of the house, to reduce the war expenditure, and I am willing to help in every movement which would make for peace in Canada and for peace between Canada and foreign countries. But international relations are an entirely different matter. As a matter of fact, international relations have produced war much more often than peace. Why? For the reason that has been pointed out by the hon. member for Southeast Grey herself, the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), namely, that public opinion in each country was directed in such a way that the men at the head of government, responsible for international affairs, either were enabled to launch their country into war if they were warmongers, or unable to prevent war if they wanted peace.
The hon. member for Nelson has alluded to that late eminent Foreign Secretary of Great Britain, then Sir Edward Grey. There is nothing more poignant than the impression one derives from reading the memoirs of Lord Grey of Falloden. One who reads that book with a disinterested mind, with a critical mind, in the right sense of the word "critical," will arrive at this conclusion: here was one man, thoroughly honest in his purpose, with a noble heart, inclined to peace by temperament, who became, under the circumstances which preceded that nefarious war, largely responsible for it. That was made quite clear in a blunt but loyal and frank manner by Lord Loreburn in his short book where, tearing down the veil

of hypocrisy,-this has no reference to Lord Grey- and all the clouds that had surrounded the conduct of foreign affairs in England in the nine years previous to the war, he summed up the whole matter in this way: Had Sir Edward Grey enlightened his own colleagues as to what he was doing, perhaps war might have been avoided. Even at the last moment, had Sir Edward Grey had the courage or the decision of mind to make it clear to Germany that England would be on the side of France or Russia, whatever the cause of war was to be, or to make it clear to France and Russia that England would remain neutral, whatever the decisions taken in Paris and St. Petersburg, war would most likely have been avoided. That is an opinion. I do not accept it altogether, although I am inclined to do so. What I want to come at is this: had public opinion in England been enlightened, things might have been different,-and may I interject here that there is no country on earth where public opinion, when properly enlightened, is so honest and! thorough as it is in England; but it must be enlightened and educated. Direction must be given to the public mind in England, France, Canada or elsewhere, so that when a grave decision has to be taken, the men responsible for the decisions of peace and war know that they can count upon an enlightened conscience; that the decision of the country, of the government and of parliament will not be stifled or precipitated by the voice of blind, ignorant, uninformed passion, as was the case in the few weeks which immediately preceded the war.
I have stated frequently and I repeat: if a plebiscite could have been taken in every country in Europe three or four weeks before war was launched, the vast majority of all the peoples, Germans as well as French, English as well as Russians, would have voted against the war. As Lloyd George has very properly said, governments tumbled into war one after another, much against their will; and perhaps not before fifty years, perhaps never, will it be possible for the historian to establish the real responsibility and say: this country or that country, this government or that government, was responsible for the war.
The hon. member for Nelson has said his mind is changed radically with regard to one of the nations in the war, the nation which the whole population of this country was taught for ten years to consider as a nation of barbarians, a nation with which it was solemnly promised we would never have anything to do by way of international trade, or otherwise, but a nation with which French, English, Italians and Americans were rushing to conclude new international contracts and to trade, six

International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
months after the war and about three months after Mr. Lloyd George had pledged hi3 honour as the leader of the British people that the kaiser would be hanged and that the pockets of the Germans would be emptied. In that respect the hon. members who have supported this resolution are absolutely right. Call in all the congresses you want; print all the peace pacts you desire; post them up on the walls of all the churches and schools; plaster all the walls of this parliament with them; erase those horrible war pictures with which you have desecrated the other chamber; cover the walls of all the big institutions with emblems of peace and love-if you do not inform the people of the preparatory causes of war, which generally grow two, three, four, five or ten years in advance, when the next fire is set, the same flame of craziness will pass over the world, and your people will force you into war in spite of all your small or big pictures.
The Briand-Kellogg pact is undoubtedly a fine declaration of goodwill. I take it for granted-it is always better to do so, either politically or charitably-that it was conceived in good faith and signed by people who wished to abide by it. But I am more sure of something else, and that is, that if those men who prepared that treaty, those men who signed it, do not take now every possible means to prepare a public opinion that will abide by that pact, when the next cause of war arises, their little bit of paper will be another "scrap of paper".
A friend of mine, an old French diplomat, once a loyal servant of the French republic, fortunately for his conscience withdrawn from the service before the war, but impelled by his conscience to utter a word of truth in the midst of lies which covered the world for ten years, began to feel his nerves grating at the constant mention of Bethmann-Hollweg's "scrap of paper". Poor Bethmann-Hollweg, one of the most honest men who ever lived in Europe and, as is admitted now by everybody who knows, perhaps the man in Europe who ran more risks and did more work to prevent war than anybody else! He wrote a book, just to tell of the scraps of paper that were torn up during the century preceding the war by those very nations, the avengers of the right and honour of the world, by France, his own country, by England, by Italy and the United States. It is a big book comprising about five hundred pages, with not a sentence of rhetoric in it, but replete with quotations and instances, all authenticated by public and official documents. It shows that every time this or that solemn covenant was
broken by the government that had signed it, every time war arose out of that lack of good faith, public opinion, uninformed, ignorant, uneducated, supported its government in the breach of faith and in the shedding of blood that followed it.
Of course, practically everybody knows today the distant causes that brought about the war between France and Pnissia in 1870 or, if you like, the wtar between Prussia and Austria in 1866. But who knew then? We are beginning to have a vague notion of the preliminary causes of the late war. In the midst of the late war I ventured the opinion that after the clouds of battle would have been dissipated, when -common sense would again come into its own, this war would likely be called the war for the partition of Turkey. It looked ridiculous at the time; but open the books that have been published in the last four or five years by the best informed and the most impartial minds of England, France, Italy, or, if you like, of Germany herself, and you will see that through all the intricacies of diplomacy, always you come -back to the rivalry of Russia and France and England at one time, and at another of Russia and Germany and Austria. Why? To divide between themselves the spoils of the "unspeakable Turk".
In 1854 such a noble man as John Bright went down to defeat -rather than betray the true interests of the British nation; but he was vindicated twenty years later by the resurrected conscience of the British people, because during those twenty years they had become informed to the point that Lord Salisbury was capable of saying in public on one occasion that in 1854, Britain had taken the wrong course, had bet on the wrong horse. His predecessor, Lord Beaconsfield did not say so. Whether he thought so in his tomb after Salisbury confessed the truth, I do not know. But I know this, that England was engaged in the war because the British people were not informed of the real causes of the war, because the history of the east was not taught in the schools of England, because the changes in the political atmosphere were not known to the people of England.
One h-on. gentleman on the other side spoke of the uselessness of confining this work of education to the universities. Others spoke of the uselessness of school education in this matter altogether, and said that we ought to put the question on its economic basis. There is something true in all those views, but they do not evince the whole truth. What is true is that if we really want peace, if we really want to sow the seeds of an enduring pacific
358	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
sentiment in this country we must make use of every agency. You think of trade? Well, I will try to show you that war is not good for trade. You are an idealist? You dream of universal peace? Well, I will try to show you that if you want to get universal peace, you must begin and work for peace at home. You think oif international goodwill? Well, if you want to impress the minds of the youth of this country with the sentiment of international good will, you must not divide the world into criminals and saints, the saints being our allies for the time being and the criminals being our enemies.
The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) referred to the time when France and not Germany was our enemy. That reminded me of the famous saying of Lord Nelson when he summed up in three short sentences his instructions to the youth of England, educating them in what he believed to be the true duty of an English sailor. "First, obey orders unquestionably. Second, revere the king. Third, hate every Frenchman like the devil."
During the late war, I had occasion, to come here and peruse some of the despatches exchanged between the government of old Canada and the British government during the Crimean war-addresses of congratulation to the queen, the sending of subscriptions for the wounded at the siege of Sebastopol, etc. It was very touching; but the most curious thing was that the very sentiments used when we were fighting Germany, from 1914 to 1918, were used in the Crimean war when we were crushing down those Russian "barbarians," those "monsters" with whom we later allied ourselves to crush down one of the most highly civilized nations of the earth. Not a nation without criminals, not a nation without faults-and here I am touching upon the point which I think is lacking in our reading of history, and that is as to the direction of public sentiment given by our press, even by our best inspired magazines and reviews, in time of war. Why not endeavour to point all the time to this basic fact, that, after all, to whatever country or race they belong, men are human beings, with faults and with good qualities? that nations have their days of greatness and their days of folly, that all peoples have had their turn, and alternately committed horrible crimes and rendered their share of service to humanity? If war is forced upon us, why not at least endeavour to come back to what was the standard of war in those so-called barbarous days of the tenth or twelfth centuries, when knights gave each other knocks on the head, but did not maintain a press 
pestering the minds of humanity and creating prejudices that would survive for generation after generation?
During four years of the war I was threatened by the censor. I was accused by the paid agents of one government or another government of being in the pay of the kaiser. Why? Because having learned from illustrious French and English authors, ten years previous to the war, that the Germans were a great people, that they had accomplished much for the benefit of humanity, I refused just because we were at war with Germany to believe that of a sudden, on the 3rd of August, 1914, the whole of these seventy millions of people had been turned into so many devils, to use the word of Lord Nelson. That some of the men at the head of the German government might have been criminals, and certainly were mistaken, I did believe, and still believe. But I thought we had some of those men at the head of our own government, that there were some in England, some in France, some in Russia, some in Austria. Because, for the first time in our history, Canada was asked to go and help in settling the affairs of Europe instead of looking after her own duties on the soil of America, I did not think I was called upon to espouse all the blind passions of the hour, and I suffered thereby for several years. It is not agreeable for a man who will have nothing else to leave to his children but the hope of an untarnished memory, to be branded all over the land as being in the pay of a foreign government; it is not exactly agreeable to be looked upon as a traitor, as one untrue to his country, simply because he thinks he can be true to his country and not become a hater of those countries with which some of the other countries in Europe are at war.
But to come back to the subject matter of the motion: public education of that nature cannot be given by the universities, but it may be given in part by them; it cannot be given entirely in public elementary schools, but it may be given by them in part. We would accomplish something for peace if we started to teach history with some tincture of Christian feeling-something that we have ceased to do for many years, not only as between [DOT]Canada and the rest of the world, not only as between England and her enemies, but as between the various elements who compose the Canadian nation-if we began teaching history in Ontario or in Quebec in such a manner that the Ontario boys and girls or the Quebec boys and girls would not grow up with the idea that the Ottawa river is such a deep abyss that there cannot be one Canadian nation composed of various elements, various creeds,

International Pence-Mr. Bourassa
various languages, respecting each other, but all agreeing to contribute of their best in common, in order to make that Canadian nation one proud of its origins, and at the same time respectful of the prejudices, if you like-I would rather say of the rights and the dignity-of other nations, even should those nations be at war with us or should we be at war with them. In other words, cannot we come back to this, Mr. Speaker? Some of us are growing old, some of us are seeing not far ahead the day when they will have to render an account for all the good and all the evil they have done in this world. I should like, when that moment comes, to think that I have done something to moderate the base passions of the people with whom I am associated and to soften my own base passions-for I have in me the roots of them as everyone of us has-I should like to give to myself and to receive from my own fellow citizens the testimony, that although I may at times have hurt the feelings of those around me, I have done it in order to elevate somewhat their minds, to bring them to think better of one another and better of other people too.
That education can and must be given by all. It cannot be confined to one group of educators or the other, it cannot be confided to one set of teachers or another. It must be the cooperative work of all the men and women who can use their influence and exercise it upon those who surround them. That does not mean that you should give your preference to Germany, or France, as against England, or that I should not have more love for the country of my ancestors than for a country which was foreign to them. No. Racial sympathies and preferences are legitimate, and prejudices unavoidable. But, I repeat, those preferences, those racial sympathies, those prejudices, must be governed and subdued by two predominant factors:	one, the law of
charity which-if we are still the Christian nation that we boast-should prevail in this country as elsewhere; and the other, that if you want to make a united people, you must stop making some of them believe that England is their motherland, and others that France is the land they should love above all. No, whether for sentimental or for practical purposes, you cannot make of this one united country, you cannot of these various elements make one united nation, one in heart, one in mind, one in purpose, unless you concentrate the thoughts and love of all upon the one land which is our country-Canada.
For that country we must be prepared to make more sacrifices than for England or France; for that country we must be prepared to conserve the lives of our people, to
preserve our civilization, instead of inducing our young boys to go and shed their blood to settle the quarrels of European nations, or to settle the affairs of Asiatic empires. This is not our duty, this is not our business. Therefore it is not only peace that must be promoted in international relations, but it is also the proper kind of patriotism that must be preached. Not that narrow patriotism which is still the curse of most European nations, but a true patriotism, a patriotism governed by the law of Christianity: love thyself first, and love thy neighbour as thyself. That is the only way by which you can satisfy the instinctive desire of a well-born people to be proud of itself, but at the same time not to have contempt or hatred for other people.
I agree to a certain extent with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that we should not interfere with education as given in concrete form in this or that set of schools. I am not going to discuss that question now, because it bears too many aspects; but I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the member for Southeast Grey, that, if this gov. ernment spends money and interferes with provincial autonomy in matters of education by seducing the heads of educational institutions in order to turn the youth of this country into would-be soldiers, it is just as legitimate to vote money to help some of the universities and colleges to educate the youth of this country in a spirit of peace and goodwill towards other peoples. One is as legitimate as the other, or one is as condemnable as the other, from the purely constitutional point of view.
But this is not the main point I want to make. Generally, I do not like very much the interference of governments, federal or provincial, in matters of education. But what this government could do would be to encourage private or collective enterprises, such for example as the Americans have done in encouraging the establishment of the PanAmerican League. There are all sorts of means by which it would be possible to encourage and foster the foundation of associations, of groups of men, who would publish reviews, who would receive documents from the various countries-a very costly enterprise which cannot be- left altogether to private efforts. This government could encourage that kind of thing. It could encourage the foundation here in Ottawa of a peace institution, of an institution making for the development of peaceful instincts, for the better knowledge of international affairs.
360	COMMONS
International Peace-Miss Macvhail
The Prime Minister has said with a good deal of reason that one cannot have a perfect knowledge of international relations unless one is familiar with the working of international affairs. Likewise, you cannot have proper diplomats, you cannot have proper officials in a foreign department, unless they have had the chance, before they get into the saddle of office, of studying history, of studying the various conditions, religious, economic, educational, under which the old nations of the world lived and still live. It is a double action, a reflex action on the part of the government and on the part of educational institutions. On this I agree with the Prime Minister: we should not narrow down' the idea of education to schools, whether they be primary schools or universities.
Without entering into details I wish to terminate my remarks by offering this thought, for their reflection, to all members of the house: let the government, let parliament, let the provincial authorities unite their efforts, or, if you prefer, direct their efforts through different channels but all with the one aim of creating one national soul, inspired, first, by love of country, and second, by love of other countries.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear the
Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) speak so happily. In places I thought his speech was highly imaginative, but at least he was in a very happy mood, and I was glad to hear him say that he agreed to refer the resolution, as amended by the member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) to the committee on industrial and international relations. I notice, however, that when the government desires to put the British North America Act in the way of its advance it is always able to do so, and when it wants to put it out of the way it is also happily able to do so.
It was pointed out by others-but I want to repeat-that the grants given to the provinces for cadet training and for technical education got round the difficulty of the British North America Act, and that could be done again. If the Prime Minister and his government want to do it I know that ways can be found. It may be that the request should come from the province or from the university, but that the British North America Act is an insurmountable 'barrier I cannot agree. The Prime Minister says we do not ask much; that is true. We do not expect very much from the government, and we are not asking for more than we think we would receive. One dollar for one hundred dollars-well, we thought that was better than nothing. The

Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) pointed out this afternoon that the government is already spending well over $199,000 for peace -practically the $200,000 which I mentioned in my resolution yesterday-but all the things that he mentioned were to promote peace outside Canada, that is, Canada's relations with the rest of the world in regard to peace, which is very excellent, and in approving this I am very happy to say I agree with him. I am speaking, however, of promoting peace within Canada, that we may have a united public opinion following what Canada is doing outside. I think we have done exceedingly little to keep public opinion in Canada well informed on what even we have done abroad, and a little later in the session I may have an opportunity to go into it more fully.
May I say again, Mr. Speaker, that we do need in the Department of External Affairs a section or a part of that department set aside exclusively for the work of the League of Nations; there we could have two or three people whose time would be given over exclusively to the affairs of the league and to giving to the Canadian people the information that they from time to time desire regarding the work of the league. We have not done very much of that sort of thing.
I am not again going into the details of the resolution. I am very glad that it is to be referred to a committee, and there the details can be gone into. But I do not take very seriously the statement made by the Prime Minister that all the departments of government are working for peace. That, I suppose, could, in the same sense, be said before 1914, in this country and every other country in the world, and yet it did not prevent the world bringing upon itself the terrific calamity that has come to be called the great war. What is everybody's business is nobody's business; when you have all departments looking after peace it is quite likely you do not get it looked after at all, and the same is true with regard to the remark of the Prime Minister that all university professors are trying to bring about peace. Doubtless they are but none specifically. I believe that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice are interested in world peace. I believe both of them are sincere advocates of peace, within certain limits. I think they would like to go outside those limits, if they felt they could do it safely. But I am afraid that is not enough. It will never be easy to begin to build up a technique of peace. It is never easy to do new things, and I notice that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice each year have a good deal to say as to what is wrong with what I propose

International Peace-Mr. Bennett
about building up a technique of peace. I am therefore going to invite those two learned and eminent gentlemen to propose ways themselves for working out a technique of peace that will develop a peaceful sentiment throughout Canada. The Prime Minister has proposed one, the framing of the Briand-Kellogg pact and putting it in every school and church. Really, Mr. Speaker, that is not a profound thought. I am sure there are many things better than I propose; I only want someone else to propose them, and I shall be very glad to give them my support. When I proposed a department of peace the Prime Minister could not say that that interfered with the British North America Act, but he said that all ministers are working for peace and that we do not need another department. We could not have that. And now when I propose professorships and scholarships it is going to interfere with the provinces the Prime Minister says; and if we get it Ferguson is going to appoint a man to teach us high protection-at least that is what I judge he meant. To be putting obstacles in the path continually is not very laudable conduct for those two ministers that I have already named, and I do think it is quite time that the government of Canada proposed something definite that will bring about the education of the Canadian people along the lines of peace.
I do not desire to take up any more time, Mr. Speaker, except to end with a very brief quotation from Emerson. He said:
It is really a thought that built this portentous war establishment, and a thought shall melt it away.
And that, I think, is true. I hope that the house will approve of having the resolution sent to the committee, and there we may at least wrestle with it for a time.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CRAIKS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADIAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to participate in this debate, because I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) at least for her sincerity of purpose, and for her consistency in advocating anything that may advance the cause of peace. Nineteen centuries have passed since the Carpenter of Galilee said, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God," and nineteen centuries have passed with human nature not having greatly changed. WTe live in an age of actualities, and in this age of actualities we find conditions imposed upon us which necessitate action being taken perhaps somewhat at variance with our own hopes. For instance, the Prime. Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to hanging in schools and churches
the Briand-Kellogg pact. The truth is that within the last few weeks the chairman of the foreign relations committee of the United States senate has made a speech that is as wholly at variance with that pact as can possibly be imagined. He said that while the pact was being signed armaments were being increased, and that vast sums were being expended for that purpose while the ink was drying on the signature to the pact. That illustrates better than anything I can possibly suggest that human nature has not materially changed in the course of nineteen centuries. Change does not necessarily mean progress, but there has been much progress toward a better understanding and appreciation of the rights of others when we are dealing with our own. However, the essential thing to remember is that all progress in the end must arise through the supremacy of the rule and reign of law; that in the end the passions of people can be restrained only as a result of the reign of law; that in the end, however much we may pass resolutions and sign pacts, it must be the supremacy of law which determines the peace of nations and of peoples. For that reason the suggestions which have been made by the hon. member who moved this resolution become important. The reign of law can be established only if you have a strong, enlightened and informed public opinion directing the agencies of legislatures and of nations. That public opinion can be secured only by education, and the means of education by which it is obtained are so numerous that it would be impossible to name them.
I hardly think it will advance the cause of peace to say that for every one hundred dollars spent for our little police force w_e are going to take one dollar and designate it as money to be used in a particular way. We must use our public money in accordance with the laws of this country as they now stand, and primary education now rests with the provinces rather than with the Dominion. The rule of law involves that until it has been changed by competent authority, we ourselves must realize and recognize the constitutional limitations imposed upon us in that regard. This parliament is not charged with the duty of elementary education. This parliament has the right to appropriate a portion of our revenues for any purpose we think desirable, but we cannot undertake to make discriminatory grants nor can we say that the money shall be used in particular ways in universities or institutions of learning which are not under our control, for they may not be willing that the money should be so used at all, and they are the governors rather
362	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Bennett
than ourselves. Our gifts might or might not be accepted, and the conditions we might impose may not be acceptable to .those in charge of the institutions. You will find some institutions throughout the world which have refused the benefits of the Carnegie, the Rockefeller and other foundations which have been established by the citizens of our neighbouring republic and other countries of the world.
Education is the basis of progress towards peace, and without education there can be no lasting peace. Education, however, is not the education of a few people but the education of all the people of the state, and every step taken in that direction is a step towards enlightened public opinion, and to that extent is educational in its force and effect. Anything, whatever it may be, however trifling and small it may seem, that gives a wider knowledge and a broader outlook on the part of the people of this and other countries as to just what is meant when we are discussing international relations means progress towards education and knowledge.
I cannot agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), that British statesmen are always wrong and someone else is always right. It seems to me this is neither the time nor the place to discuss the shortcomings of other statesmen than our own. It does not seem to me that it is our business to make unfair criticism and the very spirit of charity on which the hon. gentleman appealed is not that type of charity which attacks men who are not here to answer with respect to their doings at critical moments in the history of the world. I say that with all sincerity; this is not a time to exalt by specious argument the greatness of statesmen of other countries and endeavour to minimise and decry those of our own country. In 1914 they had problems of which we know nothing and they dealt with them as patriots. I may not know what human nature is, but in every man and woman worthy of the name of citizen there is something which we cannot describe by name which is responsive to the claims of their country, whatever it may be. Hence it was a very great thinker in a great country once remarked that he was for his country; right or wrong, his country'.
Let us take two or three illustrations in history, one early and the others more modern. Let us go back to the days when Rome made war upon Carthage; there was a very great Roman senator who closed every speech with the words, "Delenda est Carthago," or in other words, "Carthage must be destroyed". He so aroused the passions of 
the people of Rome that in the end Carthage was nothing more than a wilderness, a pile of dust on the shores of Africa. Then let us come to more modern times, when Russia and Turkey were engaged in a war to which Great Britaiin became a party. "We have the ships, we have the men, we have the money too" was the jingo song of the music halls of the time, appealing to the passions of the people. Then consider the days of the great crisis in the United States of America in connection with the sinking of the Maine in the harbour of Havana, which we now know was not the work of the Spaniards. Then we had the cry "Remember the Maine" and it appealed to the passions of the people so that the president had to yield reluctantly to the demand for war.
These are illustrations, one far back in the history of the world, one of later days and one of comparatively modern times, in which the inflamed passions of men were appealed to successfully by what you might call mass psychology and that mass (psychology is not materially changed to-day from what it was fifteen hundred years ago. We know that is so, and all we can hope to do is not to change human nature but to see that human nature has a wider vision, a larger knowledge and a Sweater understanding of what is meant by the implications of the acts in which they engage. We must learn that a simple act sometimes carries in its train results which cannot be foreseen by the ordinary man. Who would have foreseen that when the relative of an Austrian emperor was shot down a world war would result? I am sure the average man did not foresee that, although many of the statesmen of Europe did so.
If we have a properly educated and informed public opinion it may be possible so to restrain the passions of mankind that sober reason will prevail as against the prejudices that are aroused at moments such as those to which I have referred, and it is to accomplish that end, I take it, that the motion of the hon. member is made, rather than for the purpose of definitely indicating the methods by which that may be done. After all, we must remember that we in this parliament are under this constitution and are bound to observe its workings as part of the laws of this country, and I deprecate the talk which deals with the wisdom of our grandfathers as something to be treated lightly and reviled. It is not their learning or their wisdom we are discussing; we have to deal with the terms of a statute, the constitution which imposes certain limitations of the jurisdiction of a legislature on the one hand and of a parliament on the other. These are defined; if we see fit

International Peace-Mr. Bennett
to change them we may do so, and the method by which W'e may do so is also defined. However, until such changes have been made let us remember that while we may make appropriations of money, which must originate from the government for any purpose we may think desirable, I cannot see that the cause of peace would be in any other way so well advanced as by the methods which we are now pursuing in our own humble way. After all, we are but 10,000,000 people among 1,600,000,000. We are inhabiting half a continent; our own safety is comparatively secure, perhaps by reason of our geographical position, and I think to this extent I would agree with the hon. member for Labelle in that we should not endeavour to be, shall I say, the instructors of the universe. We have enough to think about in the maintenance of our own relations with other communities, and the best effort we could make in our universities we are now making in the schools of international law. The great universities of the world have chairs of international law, and international relations are based upon the rule and the reign of law. In the great world court we are endeavouring to formulate rules for the government of nations similar to the rules of law which prevail in respect to the rights, claims, immunities and privileges of individuals. When two citizens litigate, their rights are determined by principles of law and of jurisprudence, and we are endeavouring by every means within our power, as is the empire of which we are a part, so to advance through this international court the interests of world peace that nations, which are aggregations of individuals, will resort to the international court of justice for the solution of their difficulties and differences rather than have recourse to war; so that the use of the big stick, the stone, the axe or the gun which was resorted to in the early history of the world to settle differences between individuals shall not prevail with respect to nations but that they shall settle their difficulties as do individuals. The best means of bringing about the application of the principles of international jurisprudence is through this international court of justice where rules can be formulated and take definite shape, which will govern the rights of nation and nation just as we now have rules which govern and determine the rights of one individual to another.
If we pass resolutions not to engage in war, valuable as they are, they will never accomplish, as I have so often said any purpose so long as we continue to fabricate the means by which war is made possible. When we can arouse a public opinion that will insist
on the submission of the differences of nations to an arbitrament of judges trained in international problems, then I hope that armaments will disappear, but anyone who has read the history of the last two years, since the signature by the nations of the world of the Briand-Kellogg pact, will realize how difficult it is to induce nations to cease the constructing of armaments. Unless we can accomplish something similar to what is now being attempted at London, and the success of which I fancy three-quarters of the world is praying for, resolutions are without avail and there can be no real peace until public opinion is educated. There can be no educated public opinion so long as the machinery of parliaments is utilized for the purpose of providing armaments with which man may go to war.
Those who make but a casual study of international problems, as I do to some extent, may become bewildered. But thejy must realize that in moments of stress and strain, when that feeling which cannot be defined but which is in the heart and breast of every man finds expression in what is called patriotism, the love of one's country, that is not the time when reason prevails-it is the moment when blasts of passion manifest themselves. When I heard an hon. gentleman refer to the men who left this country for the purpose of fighting in the theatres of war in Europe as men who interfered with great wars in other countries, I felt that is vras not quite in keeping with the history of that movement in this country. The men went voluntarily, they were not sent;, they went because there flamed up in them that burst of love of country and its institutions and love of our empire. That is the reason they offered their lives, I for one am not prepared to say that our country should endeavour to deprive people of that spirit which has found manifestation for nineteen centuries and which I believe will manifest itself for centuries yet to come. But that feeling can be directed along the right channels by means of education, such as we are now doing through the League of Nations and with the interest we take in international affairs. We cannot do it by divesting ourselves of all responsibility to maintain a police force. The world must be policed. Who, for instance, will say that with all the civilization we have there is no necessity for policemen and courts in the cities of the world? Or who, for instance, will say that the necessity for the maintenance of a police force will have disappeared as long as this world lasts? As long as there are ships to carry cargoes of rich freight, as long as there are men actuated by sordid motives,
St. Lawrence Waterway

as there ever will be, until the millennium comes, the necessity for a police force will exist.
While the motion of the hon. member for Southeast Grey commends itself to the judgment of everyone as indicating a desire for peace and the creation of those means by which it may be perpetuated, we must realize that the methods to be pursued are methods which are limited in their operation and scope, limited because of the institutions of this country which should not be lightly overlooked.
As I said before, I did not intend to make any observations regarding the motion before the house, but in view of what has been said I would like to associate myself with the desire expressed by the mover and others for the creation of public opinion that will prevent the repetition of what has happened in former days. With the passing of years human nature may be disciplined and controlled by education as to the necessity for the establishment of the reign of law, which I believe to be the world's greatest assurance for the maintenance of the rights and liberties of nations and individuals.
Amendment (Mr. Irvine) agreed to.
Motion (Miss Macphail) as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the house adjourned the
other night I was offering a few observations on this bill, and I had concluded my remarks on the first clause, which proposes the inspection of penitentiaries by a grand jury. I do not wish to repeat what I then said, except to summarize.
Parliament in the exercise of its powers has established a system of inspection of penitentiaries which is to be found in the sections of the Penitentiary Act that I mentioned the other night. Some if not all the provinces m the exercise of their powers have authorized grand jurors to inspect provincial prisons. Parliament has done what it considered wise in its field, and the provinces have similarly provided a system which they consider advisable in their own field. It would be just as illogical for a province to pass a bill authorizing inspection of provincial institutions by inspectors of penitentiaries as for parliament to adopt this bill. If parliament is of opinion that the present system of inspection which it has authorized is not sufficient or should be improved, its duty is to amend its existing provisions so as to provide a better system of inspection under its own direction and control, but from a constitutional point of view it would be a very bad precedent if parliament
were to surrender its control of the inspection of these federal institutions and to entrust that control to a body of men appointed by the provinces for provincial purposes. That is with regard to clause 1 of this bill.
Clause 2 is intended, as is stated in the explanatory note-
To meet the cases which occasionally arise of urgent requests of relations of prisoners for permission to visit dying parents or dependents.
My hon. friend adds:
A recent case evoked wide sympathy.
The officers of the Penitentiary branch, men who have the experience, who have been in control of penitentiaries for many years, are strongly opposed to any such provision. They submit that it would be a very dangerous procedure to adopt, and one that would undoubtedly be abused if introduced. Exaggerated claims as to the degree of illness of relatives or other near dependents would continually be made and would be used as a means of securing the inmate's return for some other cause. Illness of fake relatives or fake near dependents would be a common occurrence if such a bill should become law. Many foreigners, particularly orientals, I am informed, incarcerated in Canadian penitentiaries, claim so many parents, wives, children or other near dependents that should the bill become operative it would call for a considerable expenditure of money and keep the guards busy delivering them to the homes of parents, wives, children or other near dependents. In one case alone within the past year nine orientals presented themselves at a Canadian penitentiary, all claiming to be close relatives of the one incarcerated.
They are all cousins.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Probably. The necessity for strict enforcement of the law in all its aspects in connection with the criminal is more apparent to-day than at any previous time in the history of Canada, because there is an unprecedented increase in the number of convictions for serious crimes and consequently a tremendous increase in prison population. I admit there are some cases which may evoke sympathy, but this provision would lead to such dangers and serious abuses that I do not think it would be desirable to bring about the change suggested. There was a case -and probably it is the one my hon. friend mentioned in his explanatory note-that came to my attention some time ago. The man made and pressed an application for permission of this kind which I could not grant, but what I did was to refer the matter to the Solicitor

Penitentiary Act-Mr. Lapointe
General (Mr. Cannon) who is in charge of the administration of the Ticket of Leave Act in order to see whether that convict could not be released under ticket of leave if circumstances would permit his release so that he might visit his parent who was sick. But unfortunately that was a bad case, one in which it was impossible to grant a release. That man had a very bad criminal record and could not be released under the circumstances and under the practice as it exists. This clause also, I submit, should not be adopted by parliament and the law relating to incarceration should remain as it is.
Clause 3 provides:
No person under nineteen years of age on his or her last birthday shall be admitted to or be confined in any penitentiary or other penal institution under the control or administration of the parliament of Canada, notwithstanding any law, usage or custom to the contrary.
My hon. friend said the other day that he is pleased that we are going to have preferred institutions for young convicts. As a matter of fact, this is now being worked out. The properties have been secured and the building will be erected during the course of the next fiscal year, and when that is done all the young convicts will be segregated and will have no contact with the old, hardened criminals. While this is being worked out, I do not think that this bill should be passed. My hon. friend does not indicate where these young offenders should be placed. If he suggests that they should be sent to the provincial jails, I do not think that there is anything to commend that course. As a matter of fact, evidence has been taken quite recently by the big brother and child welfare representatives as to conditions in the various jails, and it would appear from their report .that 'they certainly would not support such a change. There is not the close supervision in the provincial institutions that exists in the penitentiaries, and there are in the provincial jails old, hardened criminals who have spent their life in jail and who are associating with the juvenile offenders with a good deal less supervision than in the penitentiaries to prevent them from placing their imprint upon all those with whom they come in contact. These old criminals have more opportunities in the jails than they have in the penitentiaries to exert an evil influence on the young delinquents. This change, therefore, would certainly not be desirable while the new system of preferred institutions is being erected.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker.
I do not see my hon. friend from Toronto 
Northwest (Mr. Church) in his seat, but he sent me a note that he would not like this debate to be concluded to-night as he wished to see me about the bill, and accordingly, if I may do so, I would move the adjournment of the debate.

Just one point. Does the minister think that the question of investigation by grand juries would in itself cause difficulties? I have followed the minister's argument with care, but inasmuch as these are federal institutions there is no-shall I say?-outside check on their administration. Perhaps the minister will recall the difficulties that we had some years ago in connection with one of the penal institutions of .the country. At that time the thought occurred to me-I have not been at all certain about it-whether an investigation by a grand jury might not perhaps serve a useful purpose in connection with some of these institutions. Does the minister think the reasons against it are conclusive?

In regard to clause 3, until this new building is erected to take care of the juvenile delinquents, would the minister consider segregating these young offenders from the older criminals in the penitentiary? For years we have been reading of the great danger to the juvenile delinquent of association with the old inmates of the penitentiaries, and yet when the young delinquent comes into the penitentiary he is immediately placed alongside an old hardened criminal at the work bench. Could not the superintendent devise some means by which, until this new building is erected, juveniles when admitted to the penitentiary would be placed in a separate ward from the older inmates? 1 believe that could be done. I know that our penitentiaries are crowded, but I believe that these juvenile delinquents should be separated from the old criminals. I know of a young fellow' who was sent to the penitentiary for three years, but who after a few weeks was paroled for certain reasons in regard to his health, and during the time he was in the penitentiary he was working on the same bench with a lifer. Would the minister consider whether these young offenders cannot be segregated in the meantime? I believe that the jail is as bad as, if not worse than, the penitentiary, and I am beginning to lose faith in these reformatories As the minister says, the penitentiary does exercise a certain control w'hile the juveniles are there.
